# Front Cover

The exterior of this historical manuscript is bound in a striking decorative paper, likely created through block-printing or hand-painting. The design features bold, wavy horizontal bands in a deep reddish-maroon hue. Between these undulating dark stripes, the lighter background reveals a faint, vertical texture that suggests the use of a brush or a comb during the coloring process.

The volume is reinforced with a spine and corners made of <term>vellum<note>A durable material made from prepared animal skin, typically calf, sheep, or goat, used for centuries in high-quality bookbinding.</note></term>. This parchment shows the natural patina of age, including some darkening and small spots known as foxing, which are common in historical documents.

# Here begins the book of the reasoning of the horse
## how one should tame and govern them, and the infirmities
### and the remedies for the horse. And first we say:

The horse, in the beginning of its birth, shall be nourished continually in great abundance of milk and of grass, so that its flesh becomes firmer throughout the body and the limbs shall be larger. And this must <unclear>be by force</unclear> <note>The scribe likely means this occurs naturally or by necessity</note> when the mother has plenty of milk; and she must not be too thin nor too fat, but must keep to the middle. For if she were too fat, that fatness would so constrain the foal <note>original: "polero," a regional variant for "puledro" or foal</note> that its limbs could not properly expand—that is, grow—within the body. And for this reason, the horse [would become] too weak or thin. Furthermore, when the time comes for birth, see that it is born in a mountainous or stony place. For if the horse is born in a mountainous or stony place, its hooves will become stronger and firmer through the habit of their birth among the mountains or the stones. I say that the thighs of the horse will be stronger because of the exertion of the mountain, going up and down; and our work [contributes] to this. It can also [be aided] by the defense...

If one desires the horse's bones to grow larger <note>The author suggests that specific environmental conditions during growth affect skeletal density and size.</note> in this manner: when the mother is at pasture day and night, let her stay in a locked enclosure <gloss>and</gloss> let her be given plenty to eat and drink. Because of the time she has spent locked away, the foal would <unclear>eat</unclear> in time; however, the foal should follow the mother continuously wherever she goes to the place where the grass is, until he is two years old. And I say two years because, if this age were passed, he would immediately want to mate with his mother or with another mare. Because of the superfluity of the sperm <note>original: "supperfluita delo sperma"; a reference to the humoral theory that an excess of reproductive fluid drives the instinct to mate.</note> from the mother, he would have to do it with her, and clearly he could worsen and also become impaired <term>magagnare</term> <note>A term used in historical veterinary texts to describe a permanent physical defect or blemish caused by injury or strain.</note> in some part of his body. And for what I have said above, I concede that the horse in good, good pasture may have liberty for two years, but not before; because by going through the pasture day and night, the <unclear>air</unclear> enters into his body and into his limbs. And let him be without the company of the mother or of another horse, and this is worth much to preserve health in him, and especially in his thighs <note>original: "cosse"</note>, so that they may be clean of every blemish <term>macula</term> <note>Refers to physical marks, swellings, or imperfections that would lower the horse's value.</note>.

### On the capturing of the horse

<note>The initial letter is a decorative red 'O', though the context suggests the word is 'Detto' (Having spoken).</note> Having spoken of the birth and of the generation of the horse, now we must treat in this second place of its capturing; that is, when it is taken and when it ought to be tamed. And one must then tie it gently with a thick and strong rope made of wool, because wool is more agreeable due to its softness, or with a rope of linen or of a similar likeness. Furthermore, a man should capture the horse in humid weather or when it is cloudy, and then tie it; for if it were captured in the heat, or at a time when it should not be taken, it would tire itself too much, and because of this, it could easily lose strength in its body and limbs. And in this same rule, once taken as I have said, and especially with a <term>halter</term><note>original: "capresto"</note> of bone, it should be accompanied by another horse that is already tamed. And regarding the place where it must be tamed, we shall speak further on; because every like thing desires to have its similar, the horse that is to be tamed is tamed more safely when accompanied than without company. Furthermore, for its taming, one must be diligent to see that the horse in the <term>stall</term><note>original: "stallo"</note> should be tied with two reins, lest by its wildness in any place

In the stable, as was said above, and at his front feet, let there be two iron hobbles <note>original: "pastoie"</note> made with chains, and let them be placed there; and also from the feet [let there be] a rope which is called a "drag-line" <note>original: "trasinello"; a tethering rope used to limit movement</note> so that he cannot move in any way. And this shall be done to preserve the health of his legs. And also, where the horse stays, let it be continually cleaned of all filth, both day and night. And let a bed of straw or long, large hay be made.

And early in the morning, let all the filth be removed, and the bed [refreshed]. Also, one ought to rub the back, the legs, and all the limbs with a suitable currycomb <note>original: "stregghio"</note> as well as can be done by force and with the greatest care. And afterwards, let him be led to the water at a slow pace, and let him stay in the water—both in the morning and in the evening—up to the knees or a little higher, for the space of three hours. And let this water be cold and fresh, from a running vein <note>a spring or stream</note>, or in sea water; for the coldness of fresh water and the saltiness <note>original: "sicrita," likely referring to the drying/astringent properties of salt</note> of sea water dry out the horse's legs, because they constrain the humors <note>term: humors; in medieval medicine, these were bodily fluids believed to control health</note> and the infirmities that would come to the legs.

And when you lead him back from the water, do not put him in the stable immediately until you have dried his legs well; for the moisture <note>original: "fumosito"; literally "smokiness" or vapors</note> of the stable and the heat of the stable tend to cause galls <note>skin sores or swellings</note> and bad humors, and

This occurs if they enter with wet legs. <insert>red paraph mark</insert> One thing must not be forgotten: to see that the horse eats continuously, and that he has his food at such a distance that he can barely reach it, and that he has it down on the ground at his front feet. Because he forces himself to stretch out his neck and his body through this frequent practice, nature—being active—makes the neck and the head thinner; this will make him more pleasant to rein <note>original: "affrenare"; refers to the horse's responsiveness to the bit</note> and more beautiful to look at. Because of this, his thighs continually grow more rounded, as they are subject to this constraint of the water and this continuous eating. He should also eat barley, or straw, or spelt <note>original: "spalto"; an ancient hulled wheat</note>, and fodder <term>biada: a general term for horse feed, often oats or mixed grain</term> similar to these, which are naturally the proper meal of the horse. <insert>red paraph mark</insert> And one must see if the grass is fresh—that is, young—and also the hay and all other things without the bone <note>original: "senza losso"; likely referring to the stalk or core of the plant</note>. Let him eat the grass or the hay eagerly, because the grass or the hay delights the body; through their moisture, they cause his limbs to become firm <note>original: "raggraffare"; to strengthen or pull together the musculature</note>. <insert>red paraph mark</insert> If the horse is fully grown, or has reached a full diet, let him eat only a small amount of straw and barley or similar things, so that through the dryness <note>original: "secrita," likely a variant of "siccità"</note> of the straw, the horse does not grow too fat, but remains in suitable flesh; in this way, he will keep himself stronger and better able to endure the hardship of labor.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of equine health and maintenance, focusing on the physical condition of the horse and seasonal care.</meta>

Consider that for the horse's improvement, he should be neither too fat nor too thin, but should maintain a middle ground. In this state, the horse gains the strength that he ought to have. If he were too fat, the superfluous humors <note>In medieval medicine, "humors" (umory) were bodily fluids believed to cause illness if unbalanced.</note> would naturally descend to the legs; because of this, he could suffer some infirmity which does not usually occur. <insert>And</insert> perhaps if one were to overwork him, he could fall into further illnesses. It is enough for him to be lean, yet suitably fleshy. If he were too thin, his strength would be diminished and he would be unsightly to look at.

**W**hen the horse is of full age and has been broken in, he should be purged <note>A common practice of cleansing the horse's system, often through diet or mild laxatives.</note> in the springtime for the duration of one month. This should be done in a covered place and not out in the open air. The horse should be covered with a thick woolen cloth because the grasses of springtime are cold by nature; <insert>and</insert> if the horse were not well covered, he could easily catch a cold or indeed fall into a more serious infirmity. <insert>And</insert> furthermore, when you wish to give him barley or something similar to eat, the barley must be well prepared <note>original: "acconciare" - likely meaning cleaned or soaked to remove dust.</note> before you give it, because the dust of the barley or similar things usually causes the horse to cough, etc.

## On the shoeing of the horse
Having spoken of the things mentioned above, now we shall
speak of the shoeing of the horse, for which <unclear>I believe</unclear>
that he should be shod with suitable irons;
and they must be rounded in the manner of
nails <note>original: "longhie," likely referring to the shape of the hoof wall or nails</note>, and the heads of the irons must be light
and close to one another—that is, that the
rest of the back part at the calkins <term>rampone: the turned-down ends of a horseshoe intended to prevent slipping</term> should not be very thick,
because the lighter the iron is, the more quickly the
horse's foot is lifted; and the tighter the roundness of the iron,
the more it will help me and make it stronger.
And know that the more the iron helps
the horse, the more they become weak; and to
preserve his hoof through the habit of walking,
the horse in his youth [should be] without irons.

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues the general instructions for the daily care and maintenance of a horse, focusing on cooling down after exercise and seasonal precautions.</meta>

Naturally, nourish <note>original: "notricho"</note> him for a long time and make him hardy, dark, and strong. And take care that the horse is not too sweaty; for when he is in such a state, one must not give him anything to drink or eat. Instead, he should be covered with some warm cloth, and the sweat should be removed from his body little by little so that the heat dissipates and the sweat is gone. And it should be known that too much riding is not good; it especially harms the horse too much at night, because a sweat comes upon him that would do him great harm. The feed should be given to the horse as he is accustomed, and one must take care that he is not given too much to eat—that is, too much at night—because of the dampness <note>original: "seissedito," likely referring to the humidity or evening dew</note> of the air, which could then harm him. **A**nd riding much in the morning is very beneficial to the horse. And it is necessary for the horse to continually have a linen cover in hot weather because of the flies and other things that might bother him; and similarly, in winter time, a woolen cover for the cold, so that it does not harm him. **A**s for watering the horse, take good care: one should not ride in the cool of the day <note>likely referring to the sudden temperature drops</note> from mid-July until the end of August and a little bit beyond. **A**nd take care, as I said above, regarding cold and harsh places; because [just as] too much heat [is bad], do not be accustomed to riding in extreme heat or extreme cold, as he would be greatly endangered. **A**nd just as I said to be careful in July and August, I say the same to be careful in January and February because of the extreme [cold].

cold, which would cause him to rot. **And** you should know that to preserve the <term>health of the horse</term> <note>original: "sanita del cauallo"</note> he should be <term>bled</term> <note>original: "sanghuinare"; bloodletting was a standard medieval and Renaissance veterinary practice believed to balance the humors</note> four times a year: the first time in the spring, another in the summer, another in the autumn, and another in the winter. ### On the form of the bits

Regarding the <term>instruction of the horse</term> <note>original: "dottrina dello cauallo"</note>: Now we shall say how the horse should be accustomed to the bit. He should have a <term>balanced bit</term> <note>original: "freno de bila"; likely referring to a curb bit with balanced shanks</note>, the lightest that can be found. And when you put it in his mouth, take something sweet and grease the bit. It should be a light and gentle bit because the less pain he feels at the beginning, the more willingly he will carry it, and he will be much more willing in the time to come. It is said that the bit should be smeared with honey or something sweet, because when he finds <term>sweetness</term> <note>original: "dolcitudine"</note> in the bit one time and the next, he receives it more willingly. **And** when you see that he takes it willingly and without great distress, lead him here and there by hand, morning and evening, so that he learns to walk behind the one who leads him. And when you have done this, mount him; do it gently and lead him as lightly as you can, applying the <term>spur</term> <note>original: "sperone"</note> firmly but at a small pace.

something with him, and let him get used to turning to the left hand and to the right, hitting him gently with a thin rod <note>original: "verghetta sottile"</note> and sage-brush if necessary. This is because the horse always opens more easily from the left side than from the right. And when he appears ready, he shall straighten the bit, exerting himself so that the horse takes it willingly. ### Of the coat of the horse

**O**f the horse's coat, since they are diverse and people perceive diverse things about them, I will say that it is not fitting for a physician to judge by the coat—which some call bay, or half-white, or sorrel <note>original: "isauro"; likely referring to a yellowish or sorrel coat</note>—even if it is highly praised. **And** then I will say that regarding the similarity of coats, it is a confusing thing to give reason and cause, because each person judges as they say; and I shall leave this be.

**I**t is to be known that the beauty of the horse is known sooner and better and more clearly when it is thin than when it is fat, because through the thinness of the horse rather than through the fatness, its disposition is sooner recognized and better seen.

# The Remedy for This

Against this infirmity, take such medicine: when these glands <note>lymph nodes</note> swell under the horse's throat and suddenly cause difficulty in breathing, one must immediately place milk <note>original: "lacy," likely a dialectal form of "latte"</note> under the throat, rubbing it in with the hand and leaving it for a sufficient time as best as one can. And it is also to be known that this powder of realgar, in any such cut, regrows the flesh like fire <note>likely meaning it acts as a cautery or stimulant for healing</note> when applied upon any rupture.

## ¶. Concerning the Uvula .6.
<note>original: "uvola"; likely referring to swollen lymph nodes or "strangles" (Streptococcus equi) rather than the anatomical uvula found in humans.</note>

There are also other glands which are located between the neck and the body of the horse, that is, beneath one side and the other of the horse's cheeks. These glands come from the rheum <note>excessive watery discharge or mucus</note> descending from the horse's head, and they so constrain the horse's throat that it can neither eat nor drink, and it also cannot breathe. And they even close off the chest and the arteries of the horse so much that the horse falls down to the ground in a frenzy and scratches its head here and there, breathing heavily; it can barely draw breath. These are commonly called "uvulas."

### ¶ Remedy

Against the aforementioned uvula, let such medicine be applied: as soon as these uvulas emerge with redness and swelling like an egg or larger, they must be treated immediately with a sharp hot iron or with a sharp lancet. Cut them from the nose <note>likely referring to the nasal passages or the area near the nostrils</note> and sear them well inside, or as was said above in the chapter on the "worm" <note>referring to a previous section on parasitic or localized infections</note>. And thus let them be drawn out from one side of the cheek as well as the other; and when they have been drawn out, let them be medicated just as I said above regarding the worm.

### Of the pain from windiness

We move now to the heat in the body of the horse which comes from windiness <note>gas or colic</note> and enters through the pores of the horse due to excessive sweating. It causes the body of the horse to swell and also causes the horse great affliction. This pain is called "windiness."

### Remedy

Against this pain, the following remedy may be used: take a section of a thick reed <note>original: "bocello duna canna grossa"</DE> and let it be a span long. First, soak it in oil and insert the greater part of it into the orifice of the horse—that is, in the anus <note>original: "sesso"</note>. Then, let the tail of the horse be tied so that the animal cannot push it out. Continue this until the horse is able to pass the gas.

## Concerning the "foundered" horse <note>original: "rinfuso"; likely referring to laminitis or a systemic congestion of the limbs</note> & eleven times it occurs

There was another infirmity of the horse which occurs due to drinking too much and due to excessive, superfluous eating; and many times it occurs due to too much fatigue. Because of the excessive eating and drinking, superfluous humors <term>humors: the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed in medieval medicine to control health</term> and blood increase, and thus these humors spread through the thighs of the horse. They impede its movement and force the horse to go lame in whichever foot is in pain. Furthermore, in its gait, it can hardly move its thigh, and also when a man wishes to raise it, it hardly moves at all. 

This happens many times due to too much fatigue, as I said, because the superfluous humor or blood goes into the thighs of the horse due to too much riding. These humors easily go to the horse's hoof <note>original: "piaia", likely referring to the sole or foot</note> and also to the hoof-wall; if one does not provide a remedy, it causes great harm. Many times this infirmity occurs when any of these aforementioned pains constrain the horse in such a way that, through too much fatigue or through the overheating caused by the pain, the humors are easily dissolved through the limbs and come to the thighs. This infirmity is called "rinfuso" or "morfuso" <note>terms for founder or farcy-like congestion</note>. Do not overlook the following chapter, because these aforementioned things are of particular importance.

### cured and healed ¶ of the disease of the eyes XVIII

**I**t happens many times that, due to the aforementioned infirmity and filthiness of the body, gathered humors <note>In medieval medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids believed to control health.</note> continually flow to the eyes and make them water; and many times they bring a "cloudiness" <term>callugine: a film or cataract-like dimness of vision</term> or fog into their eyes. And many times a "cloth" <term>panno: a pterygium or thick membrane growing over the eye</term> appears, because of which the horse cannot look as it should nor see; this infirmity is commonly called "evil of the eyes."

### Remedy for this

**F**or this infirmity, let medicinal compresses be made. First, if the eyes are watering, make a plaster on the forehead of frankincense <note>original: "libano"</note> and mastic, both pulverized in equal amounts. Apply this on a strip of cloth four fingers wide with egg white, and let the cloth be long enough to reach from one side to the other, from temple to temple. And where the plaster is to be placed, let the hair first be shaved away. Keep this plaster on the head until the eyes stop watering; and when you wish to wash this plaster off, you must wash it gently with warm water.

### ¶. xx.
### **Concerning injuries to the tongue**

It happens many times to the horse <term>cauallo</term> that injuries occur on the tongue <term>lenghua</term> for various reasons, and they are very different kinds of wounds. Many times these wounds are caused by the bite of the bit <term>freno</term>, and many times by the bite of the teeth <term>denti</term>, and many times from an infirmity which is called *personese* <note>likely a local term for a specific type of oral lesion or inflammation</note>. Because of this, the horse loses the greater part of his ability to eat. If the tongue should be broken crosswise by the teeth or by the bit, whether in front, in the middle of the tongue, or behind toward the middle of the tongue, it should be cut away; for this specific incision is incurable. This crosswise cutting of the tongue is judged incurable, yet from this cutting the horse suffers little worsening, though he loses a little [of the tongue] and still suffers from these injuries.

# Of the lung. Chapter 22.

Another infirmity also happens to the horse which causes swelling on its back and generates rotten flesh within; this occurs, as has been said, due to the tightness of the saddle or by some heavy weight that is placed upon it. Often, near the bone, an old rot <note>original: "marcia anticho," referring to a deep-seated abscess or necrotic tissue</note> is generated which breaks through the flesh, and pus continually flows out. This is commonly called "percussion of the lung," that is, a defect or injury of the lung <note>original: "maghanganiamanto di polmone." In medieval veterinary medicine, it was believed that deep back sores could affect the internal organs, specifically the lungs.</note>.

# Remedy

Which infirmity should be cured in this way: that is, the swelling which has appeared there—that is, at the site of the "lung"—must be cut well into the center so that the rot may go out and be cleared away. Once as much as possible has been drawn out, let tow <note>coarse flax or hemp fibers used for dressing wounds</note> soaked in egg white be placed therein with a suitable amount of mint, changing this dressing every day for three days. Afterward, proceed as I have described in the medication of the horn <note>referring to a previous chapter on treating hoof or horn ailments</note>, and more wisely and surely, one can also use realgar <term>realgar: a toxic arsenic sulfide mineral used in antiquity to cauterize wounds and kill parasites</term> as I said regarding the infirmity of the "worm" <note>likely referring to farcy or skin parasites</note>; in this way, it is healed without any cutting and without any pain

## On Cracks .Chapter. 139.
There are also other infirmities that occur near the joints of the horse's hindquarters, specifically at the thigh and the back legs near the flesh. The flesh breaks open lengthwise and often crosswise, and every day a discharge of matter <note>pus</note> or fluid issues from those seams. These cause the horse great pain and force the hips to limp due to an excess of flowing bad humors <note>In medieval medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids believed to cause disease if unbalanced</note>, just as I have clearly demonstrated many times above in the other chapters.

For this infirmity, the following cure should be used: first, let that area be well-shaven, and then take one part of quicklime <term>calcina uiua: caustic calcium oxide used in traditional medicine</term> and a fourth part of orpiment <term>oropimento: a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</term>. ## On Transverse Cracks. Chapter 45.

There is also another type of crack in the horse <note>original: "cauallo"</note> that runs transversely <note>horizontally across the hoof</note>, which occurs due to other small cracks or sores as I have described. This crack occurs between the "quick" <note>original: "scallacarne"; the sensitive tissue under the hoof</note> and the hoof wall, which greatly impedes the horse in its gait. This is more serious than the other cracks previously mentioned because these run crosswise and cut through the flesh where it joins with the hoof. Because of this and other cracks that might occur, the horse's hooves are very badly damaged.

## Remedy for this.

For this infirmity, one cannot provide help with any ointment; instead, it is necessary to treat it with cautery <note>original: "cottura"; fire-healing</note>. Therefore, I say that the ends of this aforementioned crack should be seared with a well-reddened hot iron. By the constriction caused by the fire, this condition cannot grow further, and it will gradually become more manageable.

## Concerning the "Fig" under the foot. Chapter 54.

It happens many times that the horse's foot is damaged beneath the hoof—that is, in the frog and the sole of the horse's foot, right in the middle. And this occurs because of some iron or wood that enters that area which is called the <term>tuello</term> <note>the coronary cushion or the internal structure of the hoof</note>. Because of this, that area called the *tuello* becomes corrupted. This injury is worsened by the old-fashioned practices of farriers <note>original: "maraschalche"</note> who do not trim the hoof properly. Because of this, around the wound at the *tuello*, there grows a superfluity of <unclear>spongy</unclear> flesh which lies beneath the sole of the foot—that is, beneath the wound that is there. And because of this constriction of the hoof around this lesion, the excess flesh grows and stands out over the sole of the foot like a fig; for this reason, the infirmity is commonly called the "fig" <note>original: "ficho"; likely referring to equine canker or exuberant granulation tissue (proud flesh)</note>.

### Remedy

This infirmity must be helped in this way: the hoof which is around this wound must be cut away deeply, and this cutting should be done quite widely into the sole of the foot—that is, inside the sole of the foot.

### Concerning the loss of the hoof

It happens very often through negligence of the scabby disease <note>likely mange or a similar skin infection</note> that humors <term>humors: the bodily fluids believed in medieval medicine to cause disease when out of balance</term> gather at the foot of the horse and even in the hoof. By necessity, these humors push the hoof away from that place which is named the coronet <note>original: "tuello"; the area where the hair meets the hoof</note>. And these humors demand a way to exit, so that the hoof must depart entirely; and it falls off immediately because of the fury of the many humors gathered there. ### Remedy

Against crooked hips ¶ If the hip of the horse turns inward, whether by being placed in a certain position, or by how it stands on the ground, or by the crowding of one hip against the other in its gait; for this, the horse should be passed <note>likely referring to a physical examination or a specific lead</note> from the front. On the inside of the hips—that is, the part facing the body near its testicles <term>colglioni</term><note>original: "colglioni"; anatomical term for testicles</note>—one must make three lines on each hip. These lines must be made crosswise. Afterward, as is customary, let the horse be ridden only a little. As the hips press against one another in its gait, it will cause a "burning" <note>likely a reference to therapeutic blistering or intentional scarring to tighten the tissue</note>, that is, an excoriation <term>schorchamento</term><note>original: "schorchamento"; the stripping or abrading of the skin</note> almost like a wound. By this means, the horse's gait is healed.

# The Twenty Qualities of a Perfect Horse

And to wish for a horse to be well-perfected,
it must be endowed with twenty things:
it should be short-jointed <note>original: "giuntato corto"; referring to short pasterns, which were historically thought to provide greater strength</note> with a dry and hollowed hoof,
a good coat upon it, and a joyful appearance;
firm in its flesh and broad in its chest,
the neck long and thick with a fine mane,
a small head and wide in the ribs,
shaped like a ram beneath its forelock <note>original: "a guisa di montone"; likely referring to a "sub-convex" or Roman-nose profile, highly prized in Baroque horses</note>.
Arched, wide, and with a well-formed mouth,
the head lean and the jaw long,

It must be strong where the saddle sits;
another thing must be connected:
thick in the haunch, for this is the most beautiful trait.
Though some say there are twenty-two [qualities],
adding small ears and eyes like an ox <note>original: "ogli como boy"; large, prominent, and calm eyes were a sign of good temperament</note>.

# Chapter One, in which the division of poisons is set forth, etc.

Know that poison is the opposite of the food of our body. And therefore, just as the food of life becomes part of our body and becomes similar to that part—taking the place of the part that has been worn away—so poison converts our body, or the part of it that it approaches, into its own poisonous nature and likeness.
And it is also said that animals, which are part of the earth, convert nourishment into their own likeness; and these animals or plants, when they are directed toward our likeness <note>The author suggests that while we consume plants/animals for health, poison reverses this biological process</note>, if we were to eat something poisonous, it would convert our body into its own poisonousness. This is because every <term>agent</term> <note>The active force that causes change</note> acts upon the <term>patient</term> <note>The passive subject that receives the action or change</note>, and our substance is, in respect to the poison, like the <term>patient</term>, and the poison is like the <term>agent</term>.
Therefore, our body is transmuted into a poisonous nature by the poison, as stated above.

This false operation <note>original: "Falsona operatiō"; referring to the harmful or "unnatural" action of toxins</note> through manifest qualities reveals itself according to the variation of the primary qualities: one being hot, another cold, one moist, and another dry. The second case of this was an apothecary <note>original: "spiciale"; a professional who prepared and sold medicines</note> who, during a time of great heat, became very thirsty at night. Searching to see if he could find something to drink, he found a small vial full of quicksilver <note>original: "ariento viuo"; mercury</note>. He drank it, and in the morning he was found dead. Because the quicksilver had come out of his backside, he was anatomized <note>original: "anothomizado"; dissected for medical examination</note>. Another note on quicksilver: that which is made by the art of alchemy <note>the medieval forerunner of chemistry</note>, sublimated in a vessel called an aludel <note>original: "aluteret"; a pear-shaped laboratory bottle used in sublimation</note>, is worse than the first kind. It is more pernicious because the first kind, which is natural, often descends through the belly either by the force of nature or with the help of a clyster <note>original: "clistere"; an enema</note>. But the sublimated quicksilver, when taken internally, gnaws at the bowels, causes an abscess <note>original: "apostemacio"</note> in the heart, and causes the retention of urine until it kills the person.

Quicksilver is "extinguished" <note>rendered inactive or killed</note> by mixing it vigorously with human saliva until it disappears. However, if you pour boiling water over it, it returns to its original state and remains worse than it was before it was extinguished—though it is still less wicked than the sublimated kind.

The second mineral poison <note>original: "veneno minerale"</note> is "zelo" <note>likely referring to a form of cold mineral or vitriol</note>. When taken internally, it coagulates the blood through its extreme coldness, stifles the spirit, and causes difficulty in breathing. In this way, it kills the vital spirits.

It is manifest whence poison <note>original: "veneno"</note> comes, for it is perdition because of its firm, pernicious operation, which is destructive to the heart. Through this multiplication, the power of the poison increases; for as is said in geometry, as quantity increases, so does power. Whence, through a small amount of poison received—which converts into its own likeness whatever it touches—it increases and multiplies its power through continuous alteration. 

And the poison, even if it be small in quantity, makes its way to the heart, which <insert>(therefore)</insert> becomes poisoned. to a person of a warmer <term>complexion</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which determined a person's temperament and physical health.</note> because the heat of both <note>The heat of the poison and the heat of the body.</note> assist one another in a single effect. And for this reason, it is seen that many men eat of the same poisonous food at a single supper in equal measure; of these, some die, some escape, and some lose their hair or fall ill. 

As I saw at a supper where four men ate of a poisonous <term>mushroom</term> <note>original: "fungiaz"</note>, of whom one died immediately, another escaped entirely, while the other two fell deathly ill. He who escaped was courageous and of a "hot heart." He who died was of a less warm complexion. And those who fell ill were warmer by nature than the one who died, and less warm than the one who escaped entirely. And this cannot be by any other means than by the <term>natural heat</term> <note>The innate life-force or metabolic heat believed to reside in the heart.</note> which preserves life. Insofar as the external heat was <term>pestilential</term> <note>Meaning destructive or disease-bearing, rather than specifically the Bubonic plague.</note> and surrounding the <unclear>laxari</unclear>, all these heats move toward the social interaction of the body. Wherefore <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> said that nothing nourishes and resists evil qualities and febrile heat more than the natural heat. To such an extent, by God, it repugns hot poisons not merely by its temperament, but by its very form.

# On the Treatment of Poisoning

If a type of poison has been distributed <note>original: "spatito," meaning spread through the body</note> and is already present, give him wine dissolved in warm water and make him vomit. And after the vomiting, make him vomit again with butter dissolved in honey-water to cleanse the stomach <note>original: "magono," literally the gizzard or craw, used here for the human stomach</note>. And then give him the Great Treacle <term>Great Treacle: a complex polypharmaceutical compound used as a universal antidote</term> with a decoction of wine in which dittany <note>original: "ditamo," a medicinal herb believed to draw out poisons</note> has been boiled. Let the quantity of the treacle be two drams <term>dram: a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</term> and of the wine two drams. And do not let him eat until seven hours have passed. After this time, give him eggs with figs, raisins, hazelnuts, and broth from a very fat hen or from a lamb.

Whereupon, if he should feel burning or pain in the intestines, make a clyster <term>clyster: an enema</term> with honey-water in which duck or chicken fat has been dissolved. And once this clyster is done, make another clyster with warm sheep's milk. Having done this, give him the aforementioned broth to eat. And if there still remains a pain of "biting" <note>original: "morfegadure," referring to sharp, gnawing pains</note> in the stomach or in the intestines, then give him a little balsam dissolved in a cup of milk to drink, so that he may be freed from the aforementioned harms.

**But** if someone has been bitten by animals, immediately place upon the site of the <insert>the</insert> bite or the wound a hen, cut open with the entrails removed. And it also helps if the site is sucked by the mouth of a healthy person. And if the site bitten or wounded by a poisoned knife should be dry, do not put treacle upon it. **But** in place of the treacle, let the site be [treated]...

# Litharge <note>original: "litargirio"; lead monoxide, a common byproduct of silver refining often used in medicines but highly toxic if ingested</note> Signs

<margin>1</margin>
**H**e to whom litharge has been given to drink will not be able
to move his bowels; instead, that which used to
pass from below will be expelled through vomiting. Cure: the cure is superior to the treatment for colic <note>severe abdominal pain</note> pains, by giving him an enema <note>original: "clisteri"</note> of honey-water with duck or chicken fat, and giving him sweet almond oil to drink, and making him eat dried figs. Let him also have his stomach cooked <note>warmed or poulticed</note> with celery juice and anointed with butter. Its theriac <note>term: theriac; a universal antidote or "miracle" medicine</note>—that is, for that poison—is the seed of the spurge plant <note>original: "catapucia"; Euphorbia lathyris, used as a potent purgative</note>, crushed and given to drink in the weight of two drams.

# Chapter 8: Concerning those who have drunk Verdigris <note>original: "verderamo"; the green pigment/rust that forms on copper</note> Signs

<margin>8</margin>
<margin>9</margin>
**H**e to whom verdigris has been given to drink will
have a blockage <note>original: "opilaciō"</note> and suffocation of the breath and of the lungs, and will almost
be unable to breathe; he will have a loss of continuity <note>internal tearing or lesions</note>
of the internal members and ulceration in the intestines and
corrosive potions <note>referring to the caustic nature of the poison</note>. Cure: the cure is to immediately provoke vomiting
with warm water, making him vomit often, and then give him an
enema with donkey’s milk and sweet almond oil; then give

And if this does not help him, have him bathe in a tub in
which there is enough olive oil that it reaches
up to his stomach. His theriac is to give him two drams
of coral alone, pulverized with white wine. etc.

### Chapter nine regarding the person who has drunk ceruse, that is, white lead

->Signs<-

<margin>9</margin>
<margin>1</margin>
The person to whom white lead <note>original: "biacha"; a toxic lead-based pigment used in cosmetics and paint</note> has been given to drink will experience vomiting of white substances along with the lead itself. Their fingers will appear blackened, and they will suffer most grievous pains in the belly; they will also experience difficulty passing water <note>original: "male di potazini"; likely referring to urinary distress or bladder pain</note> from below.

Cura: The cure is to make them vomit with water in which frog-bit seeds <note>original: "seme ze de rane"; likely Hydrocharis morsus-ranae, used in traditional medicine</note> have been cooked, and afterwards give them enemas with cabbage broth and saltless oil. ### Chapter 10 regarding the person who has received burnt lead

->Signs<-

<margin>10</margin>
<margin>1</margin>
The person to whom burnt lead <note>lead oxide or litharge</note> has been given will be unable to speak and will die suffocated; their voice cannot be heard except as a leaden sound, and their lips and tongue appear the color of lead.

Their specific theriac is the branches of quinces, peeled and crushed, and given to drink in the weight of two drams in sweet cooked wine.

# Chapter 11. Regarding those who have taken blue pigment,
# red lead, or cinnabar: Signs

<margin>11 9</margin>
**H**e to whom blue earth <note>original: "terra azuro"; likely lapis lazuli or azurite used in pigments</note>, red lead <note>original: "minio"; lead tetroxide</note>, or cinnabar <note>original: "zenaprio"; mercuric sulfide</note> has been given will suffer from vomiting and dryness of the belly. The color of the vomit will reveal whether he has received the blue, the red lead, or the cinnabar. Cure: The cure for all of these is a single medicine. Therefore, give him borage <note>original: "borazo"</note> to drink with warm water in which radish seeds have been boiled, and with this let him vomit following the vomiting that nature has already induced. After he has vomited, give him an enema with honey-water and oil; push it in as is necessary. The theriac <note>term: "triaca" - a traditional polypharmaceutical "universal" antidote</note> shall be the remedy made from burnt ring-metal <note>original: "anulo brusado"; likely referring to a specific alchemical preparation of iron or copper</note>, giving him three drams of it to drink with wine.

# Chapter 12. Regarding those who have taken <insert>realgar</insert>
# realgar: Signs

<margin>12 1</margin>
**H**e to whom realgar <note>term: "resalgazo" - arsenic sulfide, a highly toxic mineral</note> has been given will have thirst with burning <note>original: "extuaciō"</note> and dryness, and a wasting away <note>original: "cōsuptiō"</note> of the bodily fluids. He may become bound by dryness or lingering illness, or he may become paralyzed and contracted. I saw and treated a young man <note>original: "zouene"</note> to whom had been given crushed realgar to eat with roasted pig's liver <note>original: "figado di porco rosto"</note>; and I saved him from death, but he remained nearly immobile in all his joints <note>original: "zonture"</note> due to excessive dryness. Cure: The cure shall be to make him vomit with borage and warm water many times, and to give him enemas frequently.

## Chapter 21: Concerning one who has drunk or eaten opium

To the one to whom opium has been given, he will have the odor of opium, so that he is forced to vomit; and this person will be lazy, sleepy, without feeling, and without intellect, and if he does not recover, he will die. **Treatment:** The treatment is to give him very potent wine to drink and rub <gloss>his</gloss> extremities with musk <note>original: "lalmitzio/almuschio"</note> and soap, and make him sneeze with crushed pepper blown through the nostrils. His theriac is crushed castor, given in a dose of twelve grains to drink, or two drams <term>dram: a unit of apothecary weight</term> with wine.

To the one to whom scammony has been given to drink, this juice of scammony will cause a defect of the heart <note>likely heart palpitations or fainting</note> and strangulation <note>a feeling of choking</note>; he will have excessive thirst and exhaustion, and a flux of the body <note>diarrhea</note> with excoriation <note>chafing or raw irritation</note> of the bowels. **Treatment:** The treatment is to give him barley water to drink many times and make him enter a bath of lukewarm fresh water; and then give him rose syrup and borage <note>original: "borage osa"; an herb used to treat inflammation</note> to use all day, and make him sleep, and make him smell roses and myrtle and those flowers which have the name water-lilies <note>original: "nenufar"</note>, and give him foods made with snails to eat.

# Chapter 51: Concerning him who has been bitten by any venomous animal. Signs.

<margin>1</margin>
He who has been stung or bitten by a venomous animal and does not know what animal it was, should immediately have the bitten place bound tightly, and apply cupping glasses <note>original: "ventose"; a common medieval practice to draw out toxins</note> with incisions, and have the place sucked by the mouth of one of his servants, and then place crushed crayfish <note>original: "gambare"; freshwater crustaceans were often used in poultices for venom</note> upon the spot. And if that limb begins to show signs of corruption <note>original: "corupcione"; gangrene or rot</note>, have it cut away if it is possible at the beginning; and if not, have it cauterized <note>original: "cauterizar"; burning the flesh to stop the spread of poison</note> by <term>h.</term> <note>likely an abbreviation for a specific medical tool or heat</note> when the place begins to harden or putrefy. According to the deadened flesh, the signs <term>q.</term> <note>likely "show"</note> that the sting was from a deadly animal. And if the limb does not begin to putrefy or corrupt, even though the pain is very intense and the venom does not go traveling quickly through the body, this is not a bad sign, unless the sting was near the heart or near a large artery.

### Chapter 93: Regarding one who has been stung by a scorpion

<margin>93 1</margin> Upon the sting of the scorpion, one should apply warm aged oil, or apply crushed garlic, or "diatessaron" theriac <note>original: "triaca de diatesico"; a four-ingredient remedy consisting of gentian, laurel berries, birthwort, and myrrh</note>. The best medicine and theriac for this is that very same scorpion, or another one, crushed and placed upon the sting.

### Chapter 94: Regarding one who has been stung by a spider

<margin>94 1</margin> Upon the sting of a spider, the juice of crushed horehound <note>original: "pomario," likely referring to Marrubium or "mela di terra"</note> is helpful, as is <unclear>ziadio</unclear>. It is also helpful to frequently apply a cold piece [of cloth] to the area. The theriac against this sting is the aforementioned [remedy] rubbed upon it.

### Chapter 95: Regarding one who has been bitten by a shrew-mouse etc.

<margin>95</margin> Against the bite of this animal <note>original: "zurla," an archaic term for a shrew-mouse or similar small venomous mammal</note>, it is helpful to bathe the wound with very hot water and have the limb buried in sand or hot ash, and to drink powdered black cumin <note>term: "nigella" (Nigella sativa), also known as black seed, often used in medieval medicine for its warming properties</note> mixed with honey.

### Chapter 96: Regarding one who has been stung by a bee

<margin>96</margin> Against the sting of bees, an ointment made of Armenian bole <note>term: "bolo armenio"; a medicinal red clay from Armenia used as an astringent and to reduce swelling</note>, vinegar, and camphor is effective. And note that he who washes his hands and face with mallow water will not be stung by bees.

# Chapter 47: Concerning one who has been bitten by other animals

<margin>57 f</margin>
**If** anyone has been bitten by an animal, and that animal has left a tooth or anything else behind in the wound <note>original: "ilo logo," referring to the site of the injury</note>, it is necessary in that instance to rub the bitten area gently with oil and ash. After doing this, apply a plaster <term>plaster: a medical dressing or poultice applied to the skin</term> made of an oil-based liniment to the site, because in this manner it draws out the teeth or other fragments which remained in the limb.

# Chapter 48: Concerning one who has been bitten by a rabid dog

<margin>58 f</margin>
**If** anyone has been bitten by a rabid dog, and there is doubt as to whether the dog was rabid or not, rub a crust of bread over the bite and afterwards give it to other dogs. The other dogs will not want to lick it if the dog was rabid; if they eat it, the dog was not rabid. But beyond this, the signs to recognize if the dog is rabid are these: the first is that the dog holds its tongue out of its mouth. The second is that it carries its tail between its thighs. The third is that it has a hoarse voice, such that it does not spare <note>original: "nō tēua," likely meaning it does not hold back from attacking</note> the healthy or the living, and it bites the masters of its own house and everyone who comes toward it, while other dogs flee from it. And he who has been bitten by such a dog, if he does not take care and is not treated within forty days, he <unclear>will perish</unclear>.

Becoming <term>hydrophobic</term><note>original: "ydroforbito"; a historical term for rabies characterized by a fear of water</note>, that is to say, fearful of water, occurs because through the <term>rabies</term><note>original: "rabia"</note> the sufferer becomes so furious that he abhors water. When he sees it, it will seem to him that there are dogs within it; and even though he may be dying of thirst, he refuses wine for fear of those dogs which he imagines are in the liquid, and so he flees from the water. And when this symptom appears, do not hope that he shall recover. As the infirmity proceeds further, he will become rabid, and then he will discharge seed in the likeness of little dogs, and every time he has a bowel movement, he produces <term>phlegm</term><note>original: "flegma"; one of the four bodily humors believed to govern health</note> from below in the shape of little dogs. This happens because the continuous <term>imagination</term><note>original: "imaginatiō"; here meaning the mental faculty of forming images, which was believed to physically imprint upon the body's fluids</note> which he holds in his heart thinking of the dog will imprint the figure of a dog upon the humors of the body. 

And know that if a horse, or a mule, or a donkey, or a monkey, or a man becomes rabid during the time of great heat, this is the cure: upon the bitten place, apply <term>cupping glasses</term><note>original: "ventose"</note> with <term>scarification</term><note>original: "scarificatiō"; the practice of making small incisions in the skin to draw out "corrupt" blood or venom</note>. Afterward, apply crushed garlic and onions mixed with cow’s butter. Give him an <term>electuary</term><note>a medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note> of river crayfish to drink. Have him bathe every day and shave him as one shaves those suffering from <term>melancholy</term><note>original: "melaconichi"; referring to an excess of black bile</note>. Have him bathe in seawater before forty days have passed. His <term>theriac</term><note>original: "triaca"; a universal antidote or wonder-drug</note>—that is, the remedy against this bite—is burnt river crayfish; give two <term>drams</term><note>original: "drame"; a unit of weight</note> of this powder to drink at the start of every hour.

## Whether the Great Theriac frees one from poisons through a hidden property or through a manifest elemental temperament
### And it is a corollary of the preceding chapter

Regarding the aforementioned matters, this question arises: Whether the Great Theriac <note>original: "triaca grande"; a famous polypharmaceutical "universal" antidote</note>—also known as *bazara* <note>likely a reference to the Persian 'bazar' or 'bezoar', implying its status as a precious antidote</note>—is curative of poison through its <unclear>ancient</unclear> hidden virtue and specific form, or through its manifest elemental temperament <term>complexio elementare: the balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry</term> and not through its specific form.

Some say that it performs this through its specific form, basing themselves on the reasoning of Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the influential Roman physician</note>, who said that having deeply considered the recipe of Andromachus <note>Andromachus the Elder, physician to Nero and inventor of Theriac</note>, the first inventor of Theriac, and testing it, he never found it to be effective except for cold infirmities through the opposition of many hot things which enter into it, and for hot infirmities through the opposition of many cold medicines which enter into it. Therefore, Galen said that the Theriac of Andromachus performed its operation through its elemental temperament. But Galen then placed the test of the sealed earth <term>terra sigillata: a medicinal clay, often stamped with a seal, used as an antitoxin</term> against the vipers, and established that it is effective through a hidden form against every poison, although more against one than against another; against some it works alone, and against others with the addition of other things. Some others said that it performs its entire operation in the human body through its elemental temperament, basing this on the weakness or the variety of its operation when it...

# ¶ The treatise on urines according to Michael Scot, philosopher
### to the Emperor Frederick
<note>Michael Scot (c. 1175–1232) was a mathematician and scholar for Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II; he was famous for translating Aristotle and practicing astrology.</note>

Lords, you ought to know that all the infirmities and diseases that come to people are by reason of the four humors <term>humors: the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament</term>, or because some of them are broken or born within the person's body according to the human frame. Such as: ¶ Blood ¶ Phlegm ¶ Choler ¶ and Melancholy. ¶ And likewise, in man there are four elements by which the entire celestial world is governed. Namely: Fire, Air, Earth, and Water. ¶ And so there are the four humors by which the human person is nourished, maintained, and governed in this world. Namely: Blood, Phlegm, Choler, and Melancholy. ¶ Know that each of these humors is assigned by nature; for Blood follows and nourishes itself within the person according to the body of the Air that reigns in the place and the land where the person dwells. ¶ Phlegm follows the Water of that region. ¶ And Choler follows Fire. ¶ Melancholy follows the Earth of the region inhabited by the person's body. Therefore, man is called in Greek *microcosmos* <note>original: "mistro chosmo"</note>, which is to say "lesser world," because of the four humors of which they are composed, in which they reign and are preserved according to the four elements of the world.

¶ Note the division of the seasons of the year
Now you should know that the year is divided into four parts of time. Namely: Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter; and so goes the whole year. ¶ And then it begins again from the head. Know that each of these parts lasts for three months. ¶ Each of these times governs its own humors, and thus they fluctuate within the body of the person, more or less.

<summary>This page introduces a medical treatise by Michael Scot, explaining how the human body (the microcosm) mirrors the universe (the macrocosm) through the four humors and four elements. It establishes the foundational theory that health is governed by the balance of these fluids and their relationship to the seasons.</summary>
<keywords>Michael Scot, Emperor Frederick II, humoral theory, four elements, microcosm, uroscopy, medieval medicine, seasons</keywords>

--- Page 208 ---
As I have stated above: In the spring, the weather is warm and humid. In the summer, it is hot and dry. Autumn is dry and cold, and winter is cold and moist. We begin the spring in March; the summer, I believe, at Pentecost <note>The feast of Pentecost, occurring 50 days after Easter</note>; autumn before the feast of Saint Michael <note>September 29th</note>; and winter in December. Therefore, in the spring—that is, during those three months—the blood increases within a person's body. In the summer, the <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile, associated with a hot and dry temperament</note> increases. In autumn, melancholy <note>Black bile, associated with a cold and dry temperament</note> increases. And in winter, the phlegm increases—that is, during those three months. And thus, a person's health is maintained if they align themselves with the spring. Summer and youth have more in common with nature; in winter—that is, during those three months—one is maintained and approaches old age.

**S**o that you may recognize these four aforementioned humors—namely blood, phlegm, <term>choler</term>, and melancholy—which abound more or less in a person, and so that you may go to see the sick to give them remedy and counsel, first note well what follows and keep it in mind; that is, know how to observe it well.

**R**egarding blood: If the person you wish to advise has too much blood, and blood reigns too strongly in them, this is what must happen in the body: there must be an abundance and appearance of heat and a glow throughout almost all the flesh. Principally in the face and in the arms, a redness appears, and they continually feel a sweetness in the mouth more than is natural for the person. Furthermore, certain small blisters appear in the mouth, and certain burning sensations are felt in the chest, which are called <term>carbuncles</term> <note>Small, painful inflammatory sores or boils</note>, because of which they lose their appetite and sleep. And their urine must be very red and somewhat thick.

<summary>This page explains the relationship between the four seasons and the four bodily humors, detailing how blood, choler, melancholy, and phlegm fluctuate throughout the year. It also provides diagnostic signs for an excess of blood, such as skin redness, sweetness in the mouth, and specific types of sores.</summary>
<keywords>humors, four seasons, blood, choler, melancholy, phlegm, medieval medicine, diagnostics, carbuncles, urine analysis</keywords>

**For Choler** <note>Yellow bile, one of the four humors believed to cause a hot and dry temperament.</note> if the person has too much choler, which abounds too greatly in color, a lemon-yellow color <note>original: "citrino"</note> must come to their face, and a bitterness in the mouth. In their face appears a white color without any redness, and their bowel movement has little smell and is of a beautiful speed. And their eyes often tear, and the hair and the nails grow quickly on them.

**On Melancholy** <note>original: "De melinchonia." Melancholy was one of the four "humors" or bodily fluids thought to govern health and personality; it was associated with black bile, the earth element, and a cold, dry nature.</note> If a person has an abundance of melancholy, a burning sensation in the stomach must come upon them, and a dark color must appear in their face. Their blood is red, but it tends toward greenness or paleness. Their body feels cold to the touch, and they are slow to work. Their feet are very cold. Their heart is very suspicious because of too much thinking, and they are very sad. **H**aving reviewed and recognized the people who are ruled by these four humors mentioned above, in this part I wish to show you how you may be well-instructed to recognize urines—both those of the healthy and those of the sick—and the condition of people according to what the first ancient doctors have set down. These doctors were the greatest philosophers and astrologers <note>original: "strologi." # On the Virtues of Herbs

**Macer** <note>A reference to Macer Floridus, the pseudonym for the author of a famous 11th-century poem on the virtues of herbs</note>, who writes of the virtues of certain herbs, places first in the beginning the virtue of **Artemisia** <note>Mugwort or Wormwood</note> and its properties—that is, the herb of Saint Mary. He calls it the mother of all other herbs. He says, therefore, that Artemisia, especially when crushed, provides a remedy for the infirmity of the "mother" <note>original: "mare," a common medieval term for the uterus</note> of women—that is, the womb—for which reason the authors of medicine call it **Matricaria** <term>Matricaria: from the Latin 'matrix' meaning womb, denoting its use in female reproductive health</term>.

What this author says is also stated by **Dioscorides** <note>Ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> and by **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author of Natural History</note> and by many other authors of medicine. Specifically, wishing to write of the virtues of this herb, he says that the water in which it has been boiled <margin>It promotes the menstrual flow of women</margin> brings forth the menses of a woman if she drinks of it.

Furthermore, the aforementioned water or decoction promotes the menses if the woman perfumes herself <note>likely referring to a vaginal steam or fumigation</note> over that water. Furthermore, if this herb is crushed and mixed with wine, it promotes the menses if the woman drinks of it. Furthermore, this herb promotes the menses if it is crushed while green and tied to the woman's navel <note>original: "chopo," likely referring to the lower abdomen or navel area</note> overnight. <margin>To cast the dead child out of the woman's body</margin> This herb is also useful for casting a dead child <note>original: "fante morto," referring to a stillborn fetus or miscarriage</note> out of the body of the woman if she drinks of it, or even if it is merely applied to the lower parts. <margin>For inflammation of the womb</margin> This herb also dissolves the hardness and the inflammations of the womb.

Whoever is unable to urinate should drink of this herb—that is, of the water—and they will urinate immediately. <margin>To cast out the stone</margin> It is also helpful for casting out stones from the bladder.

This herb, taken frequently with wine, gives great relief to those with **jaundice** <term>Interizi: Jaundice, a yellowing of the skin and eyes</term>; and these jaundiced people are those who are yellow in the eyes and in the face. <margin>For boils and scrofula</margin> **Pliny** says and praises this herb, crushed and mixed with fat <note>original: "forza," likely meaning grease or lard</note>, to be placed upon boils or upon scrofulous swellings <note>original: "strophole," referring to glandular swellings</note>; he says it is a most excellent thing to drink of this herb with wine. <margin>Also if someone has drunk medicine or poison</margin> Furthermore, if anyone has drunk a medicine that contained **opium** in great quantity, if they drink of this herb with wine, they receive great relief from any alteration caused by that opium.

<margin>To not be harmed by any sting</margin> He says that whoever drinks of this herb is not killed by any evil medicine and cannot be harmed by it, nor can they be harmed by any wild beast. Furthermore, he says that the root...

### Concerning Birthwort <term>Aristologia: Aristolochia, commonly known as Birthwort, used historically in childbirth and for wounds</term>

It is said and found that there are three kinds of Birthwort: the first is "Long," and its root is long; the second is called "Round"; the third is called *clematis* in the Greek language <note>original: "crematis in lengua grega"</note>. This was said to be of equal virtue to the "Round" variety. And all these three species of Birthwort were said to be dry in the first degree and hot in the second <note>referring to the Galenic system of humors where plants were classified by degrees of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</note>.

### On Leeks

Hippocrates, the great author of medicine, said that he cured many various infirmities with leeks. Hippocrates gives only the leeks—that is, the juice—to those who spit
<margin>for those who spit blood through the mouth</margin>
blood through the mouth. <margin>to staunch blood from the nostrils; for women who have broken veins inside the womb; to make a woman fertile if she were sterile</margin>
You can staunch the blood which comes out of the nostrils if you put the aforementioned medicine inside; the juice of leeks, incense, and myrrh is beneficial. Furthermore, this juice of leeks delivers women who have some broken veins inside the womb <note>original: "natura"; often used in medieval texts to refer to the female reproductive organs</note> and will staunch the blood. Young women who often eat of the aforementioned medicine become fertile even if they were sterile. For anyone who has an ulcerated wound, take the juice of leeks and honey and apply it, and they will receive great benefit.
<margin>for the catarrh which drips to the lung and for the cough.</margin>

Furthermore, use the said juice and it will cure this infirmity.
<margin>For those who cannot move their bowels</margin>
For those who cannot move their bowels, take the white part of the leek and cook it in good wine, but throw away the first boiling; then add more wine and salt to taste, and then drink that decoction, and it will soften the bowels.
And yet, this same drink also binds the flux <note>diarrhea</note>. If there is anyone bitten by some venomous beast, give them leeks cooked with wine and they will recover. The leek, crushed and pounded with honey, greatly helps wounds if put on in the manner of a <unclear>p</unclear>laster.
<margin>for an old cough</margin>
The juice of the leek mixed with breast milk <note>original: "late de femena"</note> dispels an old cough if it is drunk. Furthermore, the juice of the leek with the gall of a goat takes away the pain of the ear. And also this juice mixed with honey...

## Chapter on Chamomile

<margin>To provoke urine</margin>
**G**alen <note>original: "Gelenio," referring to the famous Roman physician Galen</note>, an authority of medicine, greatly praises chamomile, which the Greeks called *anthemon* <note>original: "antenon"</note>. This herb is very fragrant and short. Another herb is found which is very similar to chamomile, and this is named *amarista* because it is bitter. The authors write that three species of chamomile are found, and the one that has gold-colored flowers is the best. ¶ The first species is named *anthemon*; this has purple flowers and is larger and stronger. ¶ The other is named *leucanthemon* <note>original: "leuchatemon"</note> and this has white flowers. ¶ The other species is named *chrysanthemon* <note>original: "grixatemo"</note> and this has black <note>likely dark yellow or deep bronze</note> flowers. All three of these species of chamomile provoke urine if drunk with wine, and they break the stone of the bladder. ¶ Also, this herb purges the menses if the womb is fumigated with it; if a woman drinks the water in which chamomile was cooked often with wine, it helps her.

<margin>for swelling and twisting of the stomach</margin>
¶ Whoever drinks of this water, it dissolves the swelling and the griping <note>original: "torziori," intestinal cramps</note> of the stomach. ¶ Chamomile takes away the spots and the darkness of the face and the freckles. ¶ If one applies crushed chamomile mixed with honey, or the water of the decoction of chamomile, it helps those with jaundice <note>original: "icteriti"</note> and marvelously aids the parts of the liver <note>original: "figado"</note>.

<margin>To make the dead fetus come out of the woman's body</margin>
¶ Whoever drinks that water of chamomile with wine, it makes the fetus of the dead creature come out of the body if the woman drinks of it.

<margin>for burns</margin>

### For Good and Useful Health

## Chapter on Henbane

**H**enbane <note>original: "isquiamo" or "bisquiamo," from the Greek hyoskyamos</note> is an herb which is very cold in nature. There are three types of henbane: the first has white seeds, the second is somewhat pink, and the third has black seeds. The most noble henbane is that which has white seeds. Should anyone ask about the red variety, physicians despise it; as for the one that produces black seeds, it is considered dangerous. The leaves of the henbane, crushed and mixed with polenta <note>likely a barley meal or poultice base</note>, cure every swelling upon which they are placed. The juice of this herb, dropped into the ears, kills the worms within them and drives away the pains. The root of this herb, cooked in vinegar, mitigates the pain of the teeth for those who hold it in their mouth. The juice made from the seeds of this herb cures flowing and hot rheum <note>an inflammatory discharge or "catarrh"</note> if one frequently anoints the eyes with it. Furthermore, this drink benefits those who spit blood if the sick person drinks of it often. The seeds of this herb, crushed and made into a paste with wine, cure breasts that are hard and swollen if this herb is applied. It is also used by physicians in many plasters <term>plasters: medical dressings spread on cloth and applied to the skin</term>.

## Chapter on Mallow

**T**he authors say that this herb is called mallow <note>original: "malua"</note> because it softens the belly when cooked. But Dioscorides <note>original: "d’alchorides," referring to the ancient Greek physician Pedanius Dioscorides</note> confirms and says that it is beneficial for the stomach <note>original: "stomegal"</note>. And between both of these authors, it is confessed that it may be eaten in the manner of small herbs <note>potherbs or salad greens</note> and it greatly benefits the internal organs, the bladder, and those who have drunk poison <note>original: "tosego"</note>. Furthermore, the authors say a plaster made of this mallow bark and willow <note>original: "salegazo"</note> in equal parts, when applied, more quickly and better heals a fresh and bleeding wound than anything else.

### ¶ Chapter on Spinach
<margin>S</margin>
Spinach <note>original: "Spinari"</note> is moist and cold at the end of the first degree and is temperate in nature. It is beneficial for the lungs, the stomach, the liver, and the throat, and it nourishes the bowels very well.

### ¶ Chapter on Orach
<margin>A</margin>
Orach <note>original: "atripiçi," likely Atriplex hortensis, often called mountain spinach</note> is cold and moist in the first degree and is temperate. According to what Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard European textbook</note> says, its nature is such that it digests well and softens the belly. It is good to use for the benefit of the stomach and for an overheated liver, and for those who are yellow in the face and in the eyes <note>a reference to jaundice</note>. This herb should be used by the young as well as the elderly.

### ¶ Chapter on Roman Cabbage, which is called Russian Cabbage
<margin>E</margin>
Roman cabbage, which is called Imperial Russian cabbage, is hot and dry. It purges black bile <note>original: "nera cholora," one of the four humors in medieval medicine</note> and turns it green. It grows continually in the throat <note>likely referring to its effect on phlegm or growths</note> and provides moisture—that is, softness—and removes hardness. ¶ And other cabbages are "monsochy" <note>possibly a regional variety</note> which are more laxative; these are called "savory turnips" by those who consider them. They thicken the blood but are good when cooked with fatty meat. Their stalks are good for making a plaster <note>term: plaster (impiastro) - a medicated paste spread on cloth and applied to the body</note> to recover the strength of the stomach for those who apply it.

### ¶ Chapter on Endive
<margin>I</margin>
Endive is cold and generally provides relief from heat; it is effective against burning of the stomach and the liver and dissolves their obstructions <note>term: opilacione - a blockage or clogging of the internal organs</note>.

### Chapter on Gourds

**G**ourds <note>original: "suoche" - likely the bottle gourd or similar squash</note> are cold and moist when raw to the stomach, but when toasted they restrain the bowels. They produce red choler <note>one of the four bodily humors associated with a hot and dry temperament</note> and are very useful for those of a sanguine or choleric nature. ### Chapter on Cinnamon

There are three types of cinnamon <note>original: "Cinamomo"</note> to be found, but of all these three types, the one that is thinner with a sweetness and bites the tongue is the best and most precious. ¶ Cinnamon dries the humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health.</note> of the stomach, strengthens it, and aids rapid digestion. ¶ Whoever eats cinnamon greatly benefits the liver and purges the urine and the menses. ¶ Furthermore, whoever eats cinnamon resolves the dropsy <note>Edema or swelling caused by excess fluid.</note> which is called "tympanites" <note>A form of dropsy where the abdomen is stretched tight like a drum (tympanum) due to gas or fluid.</note> and it helps the pain of the kidneys if the sick person eats it. ¶ Furthermore, cinnamon is effective against the stings and bites of scorpions, spiders, and other similar animals if it is placed upon them. ¶ Cinnamon, well-ground and mixed with strong vinegar, clears freckles <note>original: "lentiçene"</note> from those who wash their face with it, and it helps those who have liver disease. ¶ Coarse cinnamon stops the flow of the menses if the sick person drinks it ground with cold water, taking two grains <note>A small unit of weight based on a grain of wheat.</note> at a time.

# ¶ A Good and Proven Ointment for Healing Wounds
Take <term>mutton tallow (sheep fat)</term> 6 ounces, white wax 3 ounces, turpentine 2 ounces, pine resin 3 ounces, mastic 2 ounces, <term>olibanum (frankincense)</term> 2 ounces, <term>sarcocolla (a Persian tree gum)</term> 1 ounce, <term>gum elemi</term> 2 ounces, and rose oil 2 ounces. From all these things make an ointment, and it will produce a good effect.

# ¶ Eye Salve
Take <term>tutty (zinc oxide)</term> 2 ounces, antimony 1 ounce, <term>milfoil (yarrow)</term> 1 ounce, aloe 2 ounces, and pearls <note>margarite</note> 1 scruple. Have them pulverized and then dilute them with good <term>celandine water</term>. Then place them in the sun and let them sit. Afterward, add fennel juice, celandine juice, and rue juice. Mix them together and you will make a perfect eye salve.

# ¶ White Ointment for St. Anthony’s Fire and Leg Pustules
<note>“Fuoco sagro” or Sacred Fire usually refers to Erysipelas or shingles.</note>
Take <term>litharge (lead oxide)</term> 2 ounces, <term>ceruse (white lead)</term> 3 ounces, burnt lead 2 ounces, and 1 ounce each of mastic and olibanum. The procedure is done as follows: first, pulverize the litharge, then grind it well with rose oil and common oil. Let there be 2 or 3 ounces of oil. Do this for two days, and on the third day add the burnt lead and add another 3 ounces of oil and half as much vinegar. On the third day <insert>also</insert> add the ceruse, stirring constantly. On the fourth day add the mastic and olibanum; separately add as much oil and as much vinegar as you did the first and second times. In the summertime, use rose water if you have it. If you want it to turn red, add 3 ounces of <term>bole armoniac (red medicinal clay)</term>, but keep stirring it the whole time. Grind it for 3 or 4 days in a mortar, four times every day. In the summer, place it upon <unclear>leaves</unclear> <note>original: "souza fore de..."</note>; in the winter, use it upon a linen cloth. It is proven.

From the spirit, which is called "settled physics" by the natural philosophers <note>original: "fisicha asentata"; referring to established natural science</note>. Air is one of the four elements <term>elements: the four building blocks of the universe—earth, water, air, and fire</term> from which all things are made, created, and preserved. Air helps a man to live for two reasons: First, because air is cold and refreshes the natural heat and the heat of the heart in this manner: that is, the air enters through the pores; second, the air enters through the mouth; third, the air enters through the nose; fourth, through the pores <note>the author repeats the pores as a primary entry point for cooling</note> and goes on refreshing the whole nature of the body, cooling the blood and the heat of the heart. In this way, it helps one to live. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the physiology of the heart and the vital necessity of air for maintaining health.</meta>

The virtue and the heat that spreads to all members of the human bodies are well established. Therefore, man must possess great heat. Consequently, since the heart <note>original: "corr"</note> possesses so much heat, it is necessary as a remedy that the heart be refreshed by the virtue of the air; nevertheless, because the air is hot and humid, it is the cooling and tempering element.

->**Second part: why the air helps to maintain the body of man, and likewise helps to purge the excess of evil fumes that can generate around the heart.**<-

Therefore, since one cannot live without air, we shall recognize and teach which is good and which is bad air. The air that is good for preserving health is that which is clear, without any mixture of fumes or mists. And furthermore, good air is that which the stomach drinks in lightly, and when one feels light and delicate; and when the sun rises and goes warming lightly, and when the sun sets <note>The original "collega" likely refers to the sun's gathering or setting</note> it goes cooling lightly; and this is perfectly good air for human bodies to preserve health.

Bad air is that which is mixed with fumes and with evil mists, which rise from the stagnant waters of the sea and from the rotten earth of marshes; <note>The number /2/ in the text likely indicates a second point or a specific reference in the original manuscript</note> also those that rise from dead bodies and from carrion. In such places, evil herbs and wicked fruits grow. And those who use those herbs and fruits always live with a great heaviness of the person.
