Furthermore, that air which is found trapped between mountains is <term>wicked air<note>original: "maluaxio aiere"; likely referring to "miasma" or stagnant air believed to carry disease</note></term>. Such air cannot move, and thus it neither refreshes nor cools itself. Assuredly, this type of air feels hot and thick, and it makes the whole person feel heavy. Certainly, there are few things that cause the body to waste away as much as wicked air does; therefore, a man must take great care to guard himself and maintain his living habits with such moderation and temperance that the wicked air cannot cause him harm.

Now we shall follow with how the said wicked air should be corrected, and how a man ought to preserve and govern his health. Firstly, to correct the wicked air when you rise in the morning during the <term>Summer<note>original: "Instade"</note></term>, you should have a large fire built to one side, in such a way that the fire does not overheat you too much. This fire removes and drives out all the wicked vapors from the human body that come from the wicked air, and it does not allow them to approach the principal members <note>The "principal members" in medieval medicine usually referred to the heart, liver, and brain.</note>. Stay by the said fire for the space of half an hour and take your breakfast. That is, in the morning, use a dose of <term>cordial confection<note>original: "confeto cordiale"; a medicinal preserve or candy intended to strengthen the heart</note></term> with good wine. Also, make frequent use of <term>enemas<note>original: "christiery"</note></term>, and do this every Summer. In the <term>Winter<note>original: "uerno"</note></term>, use pills—namely <term>Chebir pills<note>original: "pilole chebir"; a common medieval purgative recipe</note></term> and <term>aggregative pills<note>original: "agregatiue"; pills composed of various ingredients to purge multiple humors</note></term>—and use <term>theriac<note>original: "triaga"; a famous ancient polypharmaceutical ointment or potion used as an antitoxin</note></term> with good wine. In this manner, a man can correct the bad effects of the air.

In this way, one must guard against <term>pestilence<note>original: "pistilenzia"</note></term>, that is, from the corruption of the air and from the evils that arise from it, such as fevers, <term>abscesses<note>original: "aposteme"</note></term>, <term>smallpox<note>original: "ovaroli"</note></term>, and many other diseases that cause people to die suddenly.

### Chapter on why a man should draw blood and at what time of the year

Know that <term>bleeding</term> <note>original: "signare"; the practice of phlebotomy or bloodletting</note> discharges the humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health</note> that are within the veins that go through the whole body, as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), author of The Canon of Medicine</note> says. And a man should perform such a discharge while healthy for two reasons. The first is when the humors abound too much with blood; and this should be done to maintain health and avoid the illnesses that can occur because of the blood. The second thing is when a man is already sick, to remove the ailments. The first is our intention: that a man should act according to the teaching of the authors of physic. And regarding the second, we will look at it briefly; however, we will see a part of the first thing for those to whom bleeding is most suited. For those who have themselves <term>bled</term><note>original: "signare"; the practice of phlebotomy or bloodletting</note>, if one cannot draw blood on the first strike, they should not allow themselves to be struck again unless out of great necessity. This is because from multiple strikes, <term>abscesses</term><note>original: "apostheme"; inflammatory swellings or collections of pus</note> could arise, and one might strike the <term>nerve</term><note>original: "neruo"; in medieval texts, this often referred to tendons, ligaments, or nerves interchangeably</note>, from which many dangers follow. Then grease your hands with rose oil and work it; it is better made this way. Let it be done.

# A most profitable oil for old wounds
Take four pounds <note>original: ℔ 4</note> of pine resin, six ounces <note>original: ℥ 6</note> of turpentine <term>tremitina: a resinous sap used for its antiseptic properties</term>, two ounces of frankincense <note>original: holibano</note>, four pounds of mastic oil <term>mastiche: a resin from the lentisk tree, often used in wound healing</term>, and one ounce of <unclear>wall</unclear> sulfur. Take all these things and put them into a new earthenware pot <note>original: pignata</note> and stir it with a reed. Let the pot be well-sealed <note>original: turata</note> so that it cannot breathe, and let it boil for the space of twelve hours. Do this in a very tempered manner <note>with controlled heat</note>. Then, after it has cooled, press it out with a reed and put it into a small barrel and keep it sealed. Then use it for all needs and you will see a good result.

## Water for the limb
<note>original: "Agua per mēbro"; likely referring to a medicinal wash for a limb or extremity.</note>

Take a new earthenware pot that holds about two <term>michi</term><note>An archaic liquid measure, roughly equivalent to a pint.</note> and take a <term>miola</term><note>A small measure or half-measure.</note> of white vinegar that is very strong, and put it in the said pot. Then take one ounce of <term>Roman vitriol</term><note>Copper sulfate, used historically as an astringent and disinfectant.</note>, one ounce of <term>alum</term><note>lume di rocha; a mineral salt used to staunch bleeding and treat skin irritations.</note>, one ounce of honey, and one ounce of salt. Then boil all these things together until it is reduced by a third. Afterward, put it in a glass vial and keep it well sealed, and you will see a good result.

<note>original: "ho gēto per mēbro prouado"; 'ho gēto' is a phonetic spelling of 'unguento' (ointment).</note>

<meta>This page introduces a medieval lapidary, a treatise on the properties of gemstones, attributed to King Euax and addressed to Emperor Nero.</meta>

Euax, King of Arabia, wrote to the Emperor Nero—following the time of Augustus—a book which contained the species of precious stones: what names and what colors they have, in what strata they are born, and what virtue each stone possesses. Because that book was too large, one individual abbreviated it and made a small book that would be more portable. Furthermore, it was not granted to anyone except dear friends and to those who are reverent observers of secret things, and to those of great character and honest life. To know the hidden virtues of precious stones—the causes of which are not seen—is a very great thing. Through precious stones, not only are the cures of physicians aided, but also many fortunes come to man, according to the authors who have proven this. Nor is this to be disbelieved, for it is a fact that God has given no less virtue to precious stones than to herbs.

### On the Diamond, First Chapter.

In India, which is at the end of the world, a diamond is found among the veins of crystal. It is of a rusty color <gloss>tending toward clear</gloss> <unclear>clear</unclear> and so hard that it cannot be broken by iron or by fire, but it is shattered with the warm blood of a goat <note>A common medieval belief that goat's blood was the only substance capable of softening a diamond.</note>. With the sharp pieces of this stone, other gems are carved. This stone is not found larger than a hazelnut. Another diamond is found in Arabia, which is larger in size than the first but is not as clear nor as precious. Another is found in the Island of Cyprus. Another is found in the iron vein of Philippi. All of these attract iron to themselves, which is what the magnet <term>calamita: a lodestone or magnet</term> does; however, the magnet does not do so in the presence of the diamond, because the diamond pulls more strongly. The diamond is of value in necromancy <note>original: "nigromanzia"; here referring to ritual magic or the occult arts</note> and marvelously makes the man who carries it strong, and drives away visions from him.

<summary>This opening chapter of a lapidary establishes the divine origin of gemstone powers and describes the physical and magical properties of the diamond, including its legendary resistance to fire and its source in India and Arabia.</summary>
<keywords>Euax, Nero, diamond, precious stones, lapidary, India, Arabia, Cyprus, magnet, necromancy, medieval science</keywords>

It should be set in gold or silver and bound to the left arm.

### Concerning the Agate, Chapter 2

Agate was first found in the river called Achates in Sicily, and it is black in color and has certain white bands, and it possesses many figures, sometimes of Kings or other shapes. It is found that King Pyrrhus <note>Pyrrhus of Epirus (c. 319–272 BC), a famous Greek general</note> possessed one that had nine figures of women, and in the middle stood Apollo with a guitar <note>original: "chitarra," likely referring to a lyre or cithara</note>, which was a thing of nature and not by human art. Another is found on the island of Crete similar to coral, and it has white veins of gypsum and it drives away the venom of the viper. Another is found in India, sometimes with the leaves of trees, sometimes with figures of wild beasts; this one takes away thirst and maintains the sight. Another is found which is bright like fire and gives off the scent of myrrh. There is another that has the color of wax with spots of blood, which is considered lowly because it is found often. Whoever carries the Agate becomes strong and vigorous and a beautiful speaker; it also makes him gracious and lends him a good complexion, makes him believed, and causes him to have the grace of God and of the world. Aeneas <note>The Trojan hero of Virgil's Aeneid</note> escaped many dangers because of this stone.

### Concerning the Alectoria, Chapter 3

<margin><image-desc>A small manicule (pointing hand) sketched in the margin.</image-desc></margin>In the belly of a castrated rooster of three years, the <term>alectorio</term><note>Alectoria or "cock-stone," a mythical stone supposedly found in the gizzards of old roosters</note> is born, and at the end of four years it is perfect. It is at most as large as a bean and resembles crystal or clear water. It makes a man strong and quenches thirst when held in the mouth, by which means many Kings and princes have won their battles. This stone brings exiled men back to their homes and preserves a man's old honors and causes him to acquire new ones; it makes a man handsome and a great speaker, bold and gracious, and makes a man very lustful. It makes a woman gracious to her husband.

### On the Jasper, Chapter 4

Jasper is found in many parts of the world, and there are indeed seven varieties. The best and most virtuous is green in color and translucent. When carried by one who is chaste, it cures fever and the ailment of <term>dropsy<note>An old medical term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid.</note></term>, and it assists women in childbirth. When consecrated and carried, it defends a man from dangers and makes him gracious and powerful; it drives away harmful shadows. It should be set in silver.

### On the Sapphire, Chapter 5

The sapphire, which is a very noble gem according to the word of Kings, is of a very resplendent color, similar to the sky. It is called by many "Syrtites" because it is found near the sands of the sea of Libya in the <term>syrtes<note>The Gulf of Sidra, known in antiquity for its dangerous sandbanks and shallows.</note></term> or shallows. The finest sapphire is that which is found in Media, which is not translucent. By nature and special dignity, it is called the "gem of gems" because it nourishes the body of man and keeps the limbs whole. No one who bears envy can harm the person who carries it. This stone frees a man from prisons; it breaks gates and iron chains—and this it does with the help of a certain herb. It places a man back in the grace of his Lord if the Lord was troubled, and it is good for reconciling those in discord. It is also good for obtaining answers in <term>necromancy<note>The practice of communicating with the dead or spirits to uncover hidden knowledge.</note></term>. It restrains internal heat in a man and checks perspiration; it heals <gloss>that is, the wounds</gloss> ulcers. When crushed with milk and applied, it takes away pain in the forehead and the filth of the eyes, and it heals many vices of the tongue. Those who carry it must be most chaste.

### On the Chalcedony, Chapter 6

Chalcedony is of a pale, shining color, which is a color halfway between the hyacinth and the beryl. This stone, when perforated and bound to the finger or the neck, makes a man win his legal disputes. This stone is found in three colors.

## Concerning the Emerald, Chapter 7

The Emerald is greener than all the herbs of the world, and twelve types are found: those from Scythia <note>An ancient region covering parts of modern-day Ukraine and Russia</note>, those from Britain, those found in veins of copper (that is, those found with spots), those from Chalcedon, and those from various other parts. The best are those from Scythia, and these are carried by griffins <note>Mythical creatures with the body of a lion and the head of an eagle</note> into their nests; these are the finest and are translucent, coloring the air around them. They do not change in the light of the sun, nor by lamp-light, nor in the shade. With these, a man finds secret things through divination; they enrich a man if he carries them with reverence, and they also make a man believed in all his affairs. Those tied around the neck cure the fever called "hemitritaeos" <note>original: "emitreo"; a semi-tertian fever</note> and also the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy</note>. They comfort troubled sight and are good against storms. They restrain lust. Washed with wine or with oil, they are more resplendent in their beauty. Flat ones are better than round ones. They are also good for those who desire to go into battle.

## Concerning the Sardonyx, Chapter 8

The Sardonyx, as for its name, is composed of two names, namely Sard and Onyx, and it has three colors from those two stones: white, red, and black, each separated from the color of the other <margin>that is, it does not stick to the wax</margin>. This stone, among all stones, does not take wax <note>Meaning it was ideal for signet rings as the wax would not adhere to the seal</note>; it makes a man humble, chaste, and modest, and therefore only a healthy <note>or "sane/wise"</note> man should wear it. It is found in Arabia and in India.

## Concerning the Onyx, Chapter 9

The Onyx is similar to the fingernail of a man <note>The name derives from the Greek word for "fingernail"</note> and has five species. This stone, tied to the finger or the neck, creates sadness and various fantasies in dreams; it causes strife and brawling among men, and in young men, it generates much saliva. It is found in India and in Arabia.

## Concerning the Sard, Chapter 10

The Sard is so called because it was first found by the Sardians; it is red in color and has no virtue <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to medicinal or magical powers</note> except that the Onyx cannot cause harm in its presence. Five species of it are found.

## On Chrysolite. chapter 11.

Chrysolite shines like gold and sparkles like fire; it has a shadow similar to seawater. When set in gold, it drives away the terrors of the night from a person, as well as melancholy and trembling of the heart. If it is bored through and tied to the neck with donkey hair, it drives away demons. It is found in Ethiopia. <note>The "terrors of the night" likely refers to nightmares or insomnia, common concerns in medieval medicine.</note>

## On Beryl. chapter 12.

Beryl is found in India, and there are nine species, but the best has the color of oil or seawater. Many are carved with six corners <note>original: ".vj. cantoni," referring to hexagonal crystals</note> so that they do not appear pale. This stone fosters love between wife and husband, and it makes the man who wears it grow in stature. It strongly warms the right hand of whoever holds it for a long time. Water in which Beryl has been placed heals infirm eyes, and if drunk, it removes belching and sighing; it heals all infirmities and pains of the liver.

## On Topaz. chapter 13.

Topaz is found on the Island of Topazos and in Arabia, and the rarer it is found, the more precious it is. There are two species of topaz: one the color of gold, the other clearer and leaner. This stone is very good <insert>for hemorrhoids</insert> and it changes according to the moon. It also makes the boiling <gloss>or the bubbling</gloss> of water and oil cease.

## On Chrysoprase. chapter 14.

Chrysoprase <note>original: "crisopallo," likely a variation of chrysoprase or chrysoberyl</note> is found in India and is green in color like leek juice, but it is steeped with drops similar to gold and shines like purple. It has no other virtue according to the book.

Hyacinth <note>likely zircon or sapphire in modern terms</note> is found in three colors: garnet-red, citron-yellow, and blue. All three have virtues: they comfort, drive away sadness and false suspicions. The garnet-colored ones are better than the other two because they are more colorful and are found more rarely; among those, the...

### On the Amethyst, Chapter 16

<margin>Amethyst</margin>
The amethyst is of a purple color, and sometimes it is of a violet color. Sometimes it is similar to a pure rose; sometimes it is similar to a drop of wine; some resemble watered-down wine. This stone is easy to carve and is an enemy to drunkenness <note>The name amethyst comes from the Greek 'amethystos,' meaning 'not drunken'; it was believed to prevent intoxication.</note>. Because this stone is found so often, it is held in low esteem. It is found in India.

### On the Chelidony, Chapter 17; of the Swallow-stone <gloss>a stone from the earth</gloss> <note>The gloss appears to be a phonetic or coded rendering of "a kid day gem point" or similar, likely referring to its origin in the earth.</note>

The chelidony <note>Also known as the swallow-stone, a legendary stone supposedly found in the bellies of young swallows.</note> is found in the bellies of young swallows; it is small and humble in appearance, but in virtue it is greater than many stones that are translucent. It is of two colors: black and red. The red one, bound in a new linen cloth and worn under the left armpit, cures long-lasting infirmity; it cures the foolish and makes men pleasant, gracious, and good speakers. The black one, bound in that same cloth mentioned before, brings a man to the successful end of what he undertakes to do; it mitigates the wrath of kings and lords, as well as pride and threats. Washed in water, it heals sick eyes. Bound in a waxed or saffron-colored linen cloth under the clothes, it cures fever and consumes evil humors <note>In medieval medicine, "humors" were the bodily fluids believed to control health and temperament.</note>.

### On Jet, Chapter 23

Jet is found in Lycia <note>an ancient region in modern-day Turkey</note> and it is shiny, black, and very light. When warmed by the hand, it attracts straw; when moistened with water, it burns; when anointed with oil, it is extinguished. Carrying it upon oneself is beneficial for those with "watery dropsy" <term>dropsy: an old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention</term>, and when washed in water, it firms loose teeth. The smoke from this stone, when received by a woman through her "nature" <note>referring to vaginal fumigation, a common medieval medical practice</note>, provokes the menstrual blood. Furthermore, when set on fire, it reveals those with the "falling sickness" <term>falling sickness: epilepsy</term>. Similarly, it drives away those who have fainted and also drives away demons; it cures upset stomachs and swollen inflammations. It resists incantations and the magical arts of prestidigitation <margin>that is, when one thing is seen for another</margin>. If a woman who cannot give birth drinks water in which this stone has sat for three days, she will give birth immediately. Furthermore, if a young girl drinks this water, it makes her virginity known; for if she were not a virgin, it would make her stay entirely [distressed] and urinate almost as if weeping. But if she were a virgin, she would remain cheerful and without trembling.

### On the Lodestone, Chapter 24

The magnet, that is, the lodestone <note>original: "calamita"</note>, is found in India and is of a rusty color; it is also found among the Troglodytes <note>ancient cave-dwelling people mentioned by Pliny</note>. It has the power to attract iron to itself and is of great value in necromancy. If a man wishes to know if his wife has been unfaithful to him, let him place it under his wife's head while she sleeps; for if she has committed a fault, she will fall out of bed while sleeping as if she were pushed by a hand, and this is because of the stench this stone emits to manifest this sin. If a man wished to rob something, he should put hot coals in the four corners of the house and then place pieces of lodestone upon them so that the smoke rises; those who are inside would all flee out of the house like lost men. This stone reconciles wife and husband together; it also makes a person graceful and a beautiful speaker, and makes them believed in all their needs. Furthermore, this stone, crushed and given to drink with mead <term>mead: a mixture of honey and water, here "mulsia"</term>, heals the dropsical person; also, when sprinkled over burns, it heals them.

### On Coral, Chapter 20

<margin>Zoroaster and Metrodorus <note>original: "vinc Zoroaste e methodoro"; likely referring to the authority of these ancient writers on the subject.</note></margin>
Coral is the green branch of a plant that stays at the bottom of the sea, which, as soon as it is pulled from the water, becomes hard and red. It is never found larger than half a foot. Great authors say that it defends against lightning and storms. They also say that if it is sown in a meadow, a field, or among olive trees, it drives away hailstorms, multiplies the fruit, and makes the harvest abundant. It also drives away the shadows of demons and vain dreams, and it helps a person to begin and bring to perfection whatever they wish to do.

### On Carnelian, Chapter 21

Although carnelian is a dark stone, it is not to be despised, as it possesses virtues just as other stones do. When tied to the finger or around the neck, it mitigates the anger that comes to a man when arguing or contending with another. That carnelian which resembles the color of meat-washings <note>A common medieval description for the pale, watery red variety of the stone.</note> restrains the flow of blood, and especially that of women.

### On the Carbuncle, Chapter 22

The carbuncle <note>A term used in antiquity for deep red gems, usually garnets or rubies.</note> is red and full of color above all other gems, and it casts out rays like a burning coal; for this reason, it is called "carbuncle." This stone is called *anthrax* in Greek <note>original: "antrax"; meaning coal or burning ember.</note>. The light of this stone is so great that the night cannot extinguish it. It is found in Libya in the land of the Troglodytes <note>original: "trogoditi"; a legendary race of cave-dwellers.</note>, and there are twelve kinds of carbuncles.

### On Ligurium, Chapter 23

Ligurium <note>A legendary stone, often identified in historical texts as fossilized amber or a variety of tourmaline.</note> is a stone produced in this manner: there is an animal called the lynx which urinates, and it hides its urine under the sand so that men cannot use it for their benefit. This urine later converts into a precious stone that is the color of amber <note>original: "electo"; from the Latin 'electrum'.</note>. It attracts straw to itself <note>A reference to static electricity, common in amber.</note>, heals stomach pain, and restores color and vigor to pale men. When used, it also consumes stones <note>original: "rena"; referring to kidney stones or gravel.</note> in the body.

<summary>This page describes the magical and medicinal properties of coral, carnelian, carbuncle, and the legendary ligurium. It focuses on their abilities to protect against storms, calm anger, stop bleeding, and heal internal ailments.</summary>
<keywords>coral, carnelian, carbuncle, ligurium, lynx stone, medieval medicine, lapidary, protective amulets</keywords>

### On the Echites <note>Aetites or "Eagle Stone"</note>, Chapter 24

<margin><image-desc>A manicule (pointing hand) points to the start of the paragraph.</image-desc></margin>
The Echites, which has thick warts like an orange <note>original: "pomo ranzio"</note> and is of a white marble color; this stone is pregnant and has another stone inside itself. The eagle places this stone in its nest to <gloss>per</gloss> defend its young from small predators. This stone helps the pregnant woman so that she does not lose the child <note>original: "guasti la creatura"</note> and does not suffer pain in childbirth. This stone, tied to the flesh of the arm, makes a man sober, makes him grow rich and be loved, makes him victorious, and makes him have a good reputation among the people. It restores health to boys and girls, restrains the falling sickness <term>falling sickness: epilepsy or "gotta caduente"</term>, and if anyone has a suspicion that another wishes to poison him, let him have that person eat with him at the table and place this stone under the table; for <gloss>perciò</gloss> that man of whom he is suspicious, if he is guilty, will be unable to eat anything until the stone is removed from under the table, and then he will eat with great appetite. It is found on the shore of the Ocean sea, and in the nest of the eagle, and in Persia <note>original: "persida"</note>; which stone Castor and Pollux carried, according to what is read.

### On the Silenite <note>Selenite or Moonstone</note>, Chapter 25

The Silenite is of a green color like grass and is very similar to jasper; it changes according to the phases of the moon, increasing in substance and decreasing <gloss>scemando</gloss> as the moon does. Furthermore, this stone procures marvelous fortunes for a man and many graces. It is found in Persia.

### Concerning the Heliotrope, Chapter 27

The <term>Heliotrope</term> <note>original: "elitropia"; also known as bloodstone</note> is a stone which resembles the Emerald in color and is deeply <gloss>deeply</gloss> marked with drops similar to drops of blood. When placed in a basin full of water facing the sun, it makes the sun appear darkened and red like blood; and afterwards, it makes the water boil and overflow. This stone makes the one who carries it speak of the life of many things by divining even that which is to come; and it makes a person lead a good and commendable life. It maintains a person in physical prosperity for a long time, increasing their lifespan; it restricts the flow of blood and drives away poison. And whoever carries this stone cannot be deceived by anyone; and if it is set in a ring with an herb named heliotrope, and certain incantations are spoken over it, it makes the person who carries it in such a manner invisible. It is found in Ethiopia, Cyprus, and Africa.

The <term>Apistite</term> <note>likely Apyrites or a similar fire-resistant stone</note> is found on the island of Corinth; it is red and shining. When placed in boiling water, it causes the boiling to stop immediately and then makes it cool down. This stone drives away birds, locusts (that is, grasshoppers), mist, storms, and almost every heavy influence from gardens, meadows, and vineyards. Placed in the sun with tinder, it casts fire; it disturbs the sight of anyone who looks at it too much in the sun. It helps a man against evil seditions, and if a man has to divide something, it makes him recognize the worse part. It preserves a man in doubtful fate if he chooses to wear it on the left side of the heart.

<term>Hematite</term> <note>original: "emathites"</note> in Greek means the same as "bloody" in Latin. This stone is very constrictive. Its powder, rubbed over dim eyes with egg white and over thick eyelids, heals them. Furthermore, dissolved with the juice of a pomegranate <note>original: "pomo ranzo"</note> in the manner of an eye-salve <note>original: "colirio"</note> on a whetstone or mortar, diluted with water and drunk, it heals those who spit blood. It heals ulcers (that is, sores) when placed upon them, and when drunk, it restricts the flow of blood in women. The powder of this stone, placed on wounds, eats away the "bad flesh" <note>cauterizes or removes infection</note>. This stone, washed often in old wine, restricts the flow of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>. Also, when this stone is dissolved and used to anoint the bites of the asp <note>original: "spantese del aspido"</note>, it heals them. Mixed with honey, it heals pain in the eyes, and when drunk, it breaks the stone of the bladder <note>original: "uelicha"</note>. It is of a rusty color and is found in Africa, Arabia, and Ethiopia.

### On Asbestos, Chapter 32

Asbestos is found in the regions of Arcadia <note>A mountainous region in Greece, often associated in mythology with ancient wonders.</note> and has the color of iron; it possesses this virtue: that once <gloss>being</gloss> lit, it is never extinguished but always shines.

### On Peanites, Chapter 33

<margin>+</margin>Peanites is a stone brown in color like a root, and it is found in the land of Agatalli. It is "pregnant" with another stone which is inside of it; this stone causes a woman to conceive if she holds it in her hand, and it makes her give birth quickly and without pain. <note>This likely refers to "eagle stones" or aetites, which were believed to rattle because of a smaller stone inside.</note>

### On Sadda, Chapter 34

Sadda is a stone which originates in the depths of the sea, and when ships pass by, it attaches itself so strongly to the wood of the ship that it cannot be pulled away without taking a piece of the ship's wood with it. It has the color of prase <note>A leek-green variety of quartz.</note> and is found in the land of Chaldea <note>An ancient region in Mesopotamia.</note>.

### On Ayedo, Chapter 35

Ayedo is a stone found in a cave in Azedi; this stone can be the cause of both death and life. When this stone is rubbed upon a whetstone with the milk of a woman who has only ever had one son and has never had a daughter, it restores sight to those who have been blind for a very long time; the whetstone must be green. Furthermore, if ground with the milk of a ewe that has only ever given birth to one male lamb, it cures gout in the feet and heals fevers caused by exhaustion. If made into an ointment, it heals those suffering from frenzy <note>A term for delirium or mental agitation.</note> by anointing their kidneys. It should be kept in silver or glass and given to one who is fasting. Furthermore, if this stone is dissolved with water on a whetstone and mixed with grease, and you use it to wash the forehead of an enemy, it will blind him; and if you make him drink of this, his lungs will burst and he will die. This stone is black in color, but its virtue is not "black" <note>Meaning its power is not inherently evil, despite its potential for harm.</note>, and this stone is not affected by fire.

### On Chrysoprase, Chapter 36

Chrysoprase is counted among the other gemstones, although it is very little valued, because it has no other virtue <note>In medieval lapidaries, "virtue" refers to the medicinal or magical powers inherent in a stone.</note> except that it is used in gold ornaments. It is found in three varieties: one entirely green in color; another is roughened with drops of blood; and the third is roughened with three white drops.

### On Crystal, Chapter 37

<margin><image-desc>A small decorative flourish or pen-trial mark resembling a scroll or knot.</image-desc></margin>
Crystal is ice hardened over many years, according to what many authors say. Others say that crystal is born in certain parts of the world where winter and ice never come. Crystal, when placed in the sun with dry tinder <note>original: "fonghi sechi," likely dried fungus or touchwood used for fire-starting</note>, ignites and throws out fire. Ground with honey and given to women, it causes milk to be produced in their breasts.

### On Galactite, Chapter 38

Galactite <term>Galactite: a stone, likely a form of chalk or clay, named from the Greek 'gala' for milk</term> is a stone that is the color of ash. Drunk with mead <note>original: "mulsia," a mixture of water and honey</note>, it multiplies milk. If taken before eating and after a bath, or if perforated and tied to the neck with a thread of wool from a pregnant sheep, it refills the breasts with milk. Similarly, if tied with that same thread to a woman's thigh, it causes her to give birth quickly. Furthermore, if the washings of the stone and salt dregs are thrown in a very clean place where sheep graze, it makes the sheep abound in milk and heals them of every mange and disease. The ancients also say that as many graces and fortunes come to a man for carrying this stone as if he carried all the other precious stones. If someone holds this stone in their mouth and it dissolves there, it disturbs the man's mind. This stone is found in the river; when ground in water, it gives off a milky juice and the taste of milk.

### On Orites, Chapter 39

<margin>+</margin>
Orites is a round stone and black in color. Applied with olive and rose oil, it heals mortal wounds made by a beast with horns.

### On the Androdagina, Chapter 44

The androdagina <note>likely a variant of 'andradite' or 'androgynus,' a stone mentioned in ancient lapidaries</note> is a square stone the color of silver, and it is as hard as a diamond. It is found in the region of the Red Sea along the shore. The authors say of this stone that it has the power to bring rest to troubled and heated minds.

### On the Opthalmius, Chapter 45

The opthalmius <note>original: "optalio"; a stone historically associated with eye health and invisibility, often identified as opal</note> is a stone which cures all infirmities of the eyes. Whoever carries it upon themselves gains good vision, but it blinds the eyes of other people; because of this, many thieves have used it to rob others without being seen.

### On the Union, Chapter 46 <gloss>pearl</gloss>

The union <note>original: "vnione"; a term for a large, high-quality pearl found alone in a shell</note> is found in sea shells, and it is called "union" because no more than one is ever found per shell. At a certain time, the shells open themselves to receive the dew of heaven, from which the union is born. Know that from the morning dew a whiter union is born than from the evening dew; for from the evening dew, they are born somewhat dark. The union from a young shell is clear, while that from an old shell is dark. The more dew the shell receives, the larger the union becomes, though none are found larger than half a walnut. However, if a storm or thunder arises, the shells flee and snap shut, and then the matter from which the union should have been born is spoiled. The most noble unions come from India and ancient Britain. The whiter the union is, the better it is for decorating gold.

# Treatise

## on Chinese Physicians and on Tea <note>The author uses the term "Medici," which refers to both the practitioners of medicine and the medical systems themselves.</note>

<meta>This page continues the description of Chinese medical practices, focusing specifically on the unique diagnostic methods used by their physicians.</meta>

The Chinese Physicians <note>original: "Medici Chinesi"</note> feel the pulse in a manner that makes those who are not accustomed to it laugh. After having applied four fingers along the artery, and pressed firmly and equally upon the wrist <note>original: "collo del braccio," literally the neck of the arm</note> of the sick person, they rest little by little until the blood, which was stopped by the pressure, has resumed its ordinary course.

A moment later, they begin again to squeeze the arm as before, and continue to do so several times. Afterward, in the manner of one who wishes to play the Harpsichord <note>original: "Clavicembalo"</note>, they raise and lower their fingers successively one after the other, pressing lightly or firmly, now more quickly and now more slowly, until the artery responds to the "keys" of the Physician, and the strength, the weakness, the irregularity, and the symptoms of the pulse are discovered.

They claim that no extraordinary accident ever occurs in the constitution that does not alter the blood, and does not, by consequence, change the pulse.

# First Chapter on Scents in General. Explanation ~
## Liquid soap which is called Neapolitan

Take two parts Ash of Turkey Oak <note>original: "Cenere de Ceruo"; likely referring to the Turkey Oak (Quercus cerris) rather than deer ash, commonly used for high-quality lye</note>, one part quicklime, and half a part of soda ash <note>original: "alume de Catina" or "cenere de leuante"; these are alkaline ashes derived from saltwort plants imported from the Levant, essential for soap making</note>. Let these things be ground and mixed well together; put them into a large basin and moisten them with fresh water until they are quite damp and mixed. Then put the mixture into a bucket that has two or three holes in the bottom. But first, place a layer of straw at the bottom of the bucket. Then throw your material on top and stomp it and press it down very tightly with the palm of your hand, especially around the sides so that it is well layered. Then pour enough fresh water into the bucket over your material so that it stands four good fingers' breadth or more above it. Let said water strain down through the holes and collect it in an earthenware basin; save it aside because it is the best and the strongest <insert>lye</insert>. Then pour more fresh water into the bucket and let it strain into another basin, and put

If it should be a burden to you to make the said water <note>The "water" refers to the caustic lye solution described on the previous page.</note>, take **master lye** <term>maistra: the strongest, first-run lye from the leaching process</term> or lye for making soap of the first and best quality; you will find it at the **soap-makers'** shops. And temper that according to your judgment, as I have told you, with other weaker water that they keep. And once it has been tempered, put it into a cauldron that is very clean—20 pounds of it—and **deer fat**, or **veal fat**, or **ram fat**—1 pound or more. 

But first, it is necessary that the fat be boiled in water and well-strained beforehand, so that it is clean of skins and small nerves. And put it together with the lye in the cauldron, and then set it over a fire of soft wood and let it boil very slowly for half an hour. 

Then, having removed it from the fire and let it cool somewhat, and while still seeing it in this state, pour everything into a **earthenware basin** that is well-glazed <note>original: "ueriato"</note> and has a very wide bottom; have it made specifically for this purpose. 

And place it in the very hot **summer sun** <note>original: "Instad"</note> and stir it every day, every hour, as much as you can; it will be seen to be thickening. And when it is well-thickened, make it into large cakes <note>original: "pani," literally loaves</note> at your pleasure. And keep them in a chest, for the older they are, the better they become. And if you should be in winter, let it boil longer upon the fire...

### Dissolved Musk for all purposes

### Powder of Cyprus, an excellent thing.

Take the skins or "eyes" <note>likely the moss or lichen known as Oakmoss</note> of Oak stalks <term>cauolli de Rouere</term><note>literally "oak cabbages," referring to the tufted lichen growth found on oak trees</note>, specifically the long ones. The human body, since it is composed through the coming together of its contrary elements, is not permanent, as the elder philosopher Plato says in his book called *The Banquet* <note>original: "de cōvīvijs"; referring to the Symposium</note>; rather, it is easily dissolved and corrupted. This is because one part is properly opposed to another and flees from it, for which reason, over a long period of time, the body is stripped of its natural composition and returns to its simple state, namely to its elements. As Constantine <note>Constantine the African, a 11th-century translator of Arabic medicine into Latin.</note> says regarding the elements: heat returns into fire, breath into air, the humors into water, and the bones and flesh into earth. And because of its composition and its reception of the traces of nature's fire, the body becomes receptive to alteration. Isaac <note>Isaac Israeli, a 10th-century Jewish physician and philosopher.</note> says that in a short time it will be dissolved due to corrupting accidents <term>accidents: in medieval medicine, these are external factors or symptoms that affect the body's health</term> which drag the body itself away from the spirit of temperance. For whatever has more parts in its composition has more defects and is more easily corrupted, as the same philosopher said. Therefore, to repel such corrupting accidents, as the Wise Man says, the Most High created medicine.

### Chapter on the generation of the human body and its composition

Truly, because as the same philosopher says, he who is ignorant of the cause cannot successfully drive away the accident. Therefore, let us first look at the composition of the human body, its qualities, and from what things it is constituted, so that a practitioner, understanding the cause, may more easily drive away its accidents. Constantine, in his commentary on youth and generation, says: Generation is a thing <unclear>made</unclear> that was not there before, which in the body of an animal was a mutation of the seed <note>original: "spermatis"</note>. From this, all members and qualities are transformed. Therefore, the human body is generated from the seed, which is hot and moist. And since things are not generated except according to their like, it is necessarily required that man be naturally hot <insert>and moist</insert>.

And thus, both naturally and accidentally, four humors <term>humors: the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament</term> are generated in the body. Since the secondary elements take their nature from the intermediate ones:
* Just as air is generated through heat and moisture, so **blood** is generated in the body of an animal.
* Just as fire is generated through heat and dryness, so is **choler** <note>yellow bile</note> generated by the same.
* Just as water is generated through cold and moisture, so is **phlegm**.
* Just as earth is generated through cold and dryness, so is **melancholy** <note>black bile</note>.

And since blood is hot and moist, it appears red and thick; red because of the heat and thick because of the moisture. Therefore, the urine of such a person is red and, as it were, generally dry in appearance, similar to the blood itself. Phlegm, since it is cold, is white; and because it is moist, it is thick; the urine of such a person appears similar to it. Melancholy, because it is dry, is white <note>The author likely refers to a pale or "leaden" clarity here</note>; because it is generally dry, the urine of such a person appears similar. The more that heat prevails in the body, the redder the urine will become. And if dryness prevails, the more thin and clear it will be. If moisture prevails, the more thick it will be. If coldness prevails, the more white it will be, and vice versa, for they say it shall so appear. And thus the colors and signs correspond. The form, whether at the top or the bottom, denotes a disease in the upper or lower part of the body. For example, when the urine is clear from the bottom up to the middle, and from that middle to the top it is thick and disturbed, it denotes a heaviness of the chest <note>This refers to the practice of dividing the uroscopy flask into regions representing the head, chest, and abdomen</note>. And so it is with similar cases. And a certain general sign of disease is when its opposite appears; for instance, if one who has an acute fever has red and thick urine at the beginning, and afterwards it becomes white and clear, it denotes an affliction of the head. <gloss>Macer</gloss> <note>original: "macer"; likely referring to Macer Floridus, a medieval authority on herbs and medicine</note>.

The **Sanguine** person, because he is hot, becomes large, and because he is moist, becomes fat. <gloss>Macer</gloss>. The **Choleric** person, because he is hot, is large, and because he is dry, becomes thin. The **Phlegmatic** person, because he is moist, becomes fat, but because he is cold, he is small. The **Melancholic** person, because he is cold, is small, and because he is dry, is thin. And this is the natural state. But by accident, a Choleric might be fat, and the Sanguine and Phlegmatic might be thin, according to their temperaments.

Furthermore, the Sanguine person, because he is hot, has a strong appetite, and because he is moist, he achieves the effect <note>likely referring to digestion or physical growth</note>. The Choleric, because he is hot, has an appetite, but his dryness hinders its effect. The Phlegmatic, because he is cold, does not have an appetite, but because he is moist, he achieves the effect. The Melancholic, because he is cold, does not have an appetite, and because he is dry, his effect is hindered. To whom excessive phlegm is harmful, because being cold he has no appetite, but being moist he achieves the effect. The Melancholic, because he is cold, has no appetite, and because he is dry, his effect is hindered; to whom everything is harmful.

The body of man is governed by the **spirit** <term>spirit: in medieval medicine, a subtle substance or "pneuma" that carries life force through the body</term>, which is threefold, as **Constantine** <note>Constantine the African (c. 1020–1087), a physician who translated Arabic medical texts into Latin</note> says in his book *On Spirits*, namely: the **natural**, the **spiritual**, and the **animal** <note>original: "nat̄ spūal' et ammal"; these correspond to the three centers of the body: the liver (natural), the heart (spiritual), and the brain (animal/mental)</note>.

The **natural spirit** <note>Latin: *spiritus naturalis*. The **spiritual spirit** <note>Latin: *spiritus spiritualis*, often associated with the "vital" spirit in other texts.</note>, however, is born in the heart and travels through the arteries to the limbs of the entire body. It governs and increases the spiritual power and guards its actions. And it is called the **corporeal soul**, although some say that it is the instrument of the soul, and in man it is as much natural as it is accidental. But because the natural spirit fails when food is lacking—and consequently this would lead to the destruction of its composite <note>The "composite" refers to the unified body and soul.</note>—therefore the same **Philosopher** <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, often cited simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval texts.</note> says that the great and sublime God placed within us a portion of appetite for food, so that it might be occupied with the finding of natural spirit, lest it harm the natural or rational soul.

And when it is deprived of natural nourishment, it cries out to its own containment and to the harm of the animal spirit, and continues and leads toward destruction. Indeed, as long as it is within us through a moist separation, it is impossible for the soul to be separated from the body; for life stands by **moisture** and death by **dryness**. They have observed that all composite things, both above <note>referring to the celestial spheres</note> and below <note>referring to the earthly realm</note>, consist of elements and qualities. These things agree with one another in their manner and are consumed together. When they agree, they are helpful; when they are consumed <note>or perhaps "clash," original: *consuantur*</note>, they are harmful. 

For example: 
Blood is hot and moist, just as the planet Jupiter is hot and moist. Jupiter creates, increases, rules, and regards blood as its dwelling place. The season of Spring is also hot and moist. Therefore, because it agrees with these, it is friendly to those qualities; thus, at that time, the blood rejoices and is increased. 

If, therefore, the blood should dominate the other humors more than is expedient because of its increase, you should choose a time in which the planet regarding that harmful humor is in a bad state or is weakened, such as being in a cold and dry sign. If, however, there is too little blood and you wish to increase it, you assist that planet while it is in a good sign of a similar nature—namely, hot and moist. 

**Saturn** is cold and dry and has an aspect toward **Melancholy** <note>Black bile; the humor associated with introspection or depression</note>; it generates, increases, and contains the spleen, which is the dwelling place of melancholy. It agrees with Autumn and with cold and dry signs. 

**The Sun and Mars** are hot and dry and have an aspect toward **Choler** <note>Yellow bile; the humor associated with anger and energy</note>; they generate and increase it. They contain the gallbladder, which is the dwelling place of choler, and they agree with Summer and with hot and dry signs. 

**The Moon** is cold and moist and regards **Phlegm**; she generates and increases it. She has an aspect toward the lungs, the dwelling place of phlegm, and agrees with Winter and with cold and moist signs. 

All these things mentioned above must be considered and diligently examined, both in the act of healing and in the preparation of medicine.

Let it be one <term>high-combining</term><note>original: "altacōmbus," likely a corruption of a term referring to the alchemical process of sublimation or union</note> and so that the world which is in it may be separated from unclean filth and reduced, as it were, to a simple state. Wherefore **Avicenna** says in his book on the *Distinctions of Waters* that the boiling of water removes the thickness of cold and causes that which is corrupted in it to descend; hence sublimation and distillation rectify bad waters, and the earthy part is separated from it, and there remains pure and simple water. And that which was separated through heating will be
<margin>Homogeneous</margin>
<term>homogeneous</term><note>original: "lymogonium," interpreted here as homogeneous based on the marginal note</note>, that is, one and the same with that which remained. And the cause of the descent is the subtlety which is acquired from the boiling; it is separated gradually and not quickly. For thick mixtures easily descend from a subtle substance in which there is no thickness, nor viscosity, nor oiliness; but from a thickened substance they do not descend easily at all. Therefore, boiling truly acquires subtlety through the gathering of the pre-boiling process. **Plato** says secondly that things of a high-combining nature return to their own form and nature, which then is assimilated to it. When a thing has been such in its nature, it follows that corruption does not happen to it, because corruption and annihilation proceed from contrary things. Thus you see rot in an apple, and the union in a fire consuming wood. But since corruption does not have the possibility of penetrating a thing from its own contrary nature, it does not enter the matter. Thus it makes a simple thing in which the clear part is separated from the dregs, and through this inseparability, it has obtained the name of "the clear of the immortals." Moreover, a thing reduced to a simple and clear state does not lose any of its properties, but converts them totally from their own form to its own essence or nature. Deservedly, therefore, wine reduced to a clear state and separated from its dregs is called the marvelous **Water of Life** <note>original: "aqua vite"</note>, possessing the power and virtue of **Burning Water** <note>original: "aq̄ ardētis"</note>.

# On the Aspects of the Moon

Now we must speak of the parts of the body which the moon rules and toward which it directs its influence <note>original: "aspectum"</note> while it is in the sign of **Taurus**, which are the neck, the throat, and the shoulder blades. When the moon is under that sign, it dominates those parts. The neck is the "column of the head," perforated so that food and drink may enter to serve nature; as the same Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in medieval texts.</note> says, nature is nourished by drink. It is the height of the breath <note>original: "altitudo amme," likely referring to the windpipe or the 'pneuma'</note> and the form of forms and the genus of genera.

If, therefore, the moon is positioned under this sign, let the columbine lily <note>term: "lilu' columbina" (Aquilegia vulgaris), used in medieval medicine for throat ailments</note> be gathered, or let it be mixed with water. ...they take [it] up / and in the heart they receive growth <note>original: "incrementum"</note> through use.
And **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus, a highly influential Roman physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> says: From the movement of the spirit of the heart proceeds the pulse, and more suitably on the left side than on the right. For when the pulse is strong and slow, it signifies an abundance of **blood**, because heat is strong and moisture is slow. However, when it is strong and fast, it denotes an abundance of **choler** <note>also known as yellow bile</note>. Because it is hot, it is strong; because it is dry, it is fast. But when it is slow and weak, it denotes an abundance of **phlegm**, because cold is weak and moisture is slow. But when it is weak and fast, it denotes **melancholy** <note>also known as black bile</note>. Because it is cold, it is weak; because it is dry, it is fast. Nevertheless, it moves more or less according to the age of the man, the composition of regions, the changes of the seasons and places, and the varieties of food and drink.

Because in the **spring**, blood reigns more supreme. And in the **summer**, choler. And in the **autumn**, melancholy. And in the **winter**, phlegm. And in any given day, from the ninth hour of the night until the third hour of the day, blood reigns. From the third hour of the day until the ninth hour of the day, choler reigns. From the ninth hour of the day until the third hour of the night, phlegm <note>The text here attributes phlegm to the evening, though some traditions vary</note>. And from the third hour of the night until the ninth hour of the night, melancholy reigns. Whence:

In spring, the pulses are strong and slow. In summer, strong and fast. In autumn, weak and fast. In winter, weak and slow. Moisture does not act as strongly against its opposite as heat does against cold. Therefore, the signs are not as strongly opposed from point A to point A.

# In the name of the Lord, amen. Here begins the treatise
# on the magnetic stone

<margin>On the Artifice of Perpetual Motion.</margin>
This treatise on the magnet contains two parts, the first of which is completed in ten chapters and the second in three. The first chapter of the first part concerns the purpose of the work; the second, what kind of craftsman this work requires; the third, on the recognition of the stone; the fourth, on the science of investigating the parts of the stone; the fifth, on the science of investigating the poles in the stone, namely which of them is North and which is South; the sixth, how a magnet attracts a magnet; the seventh, how iron touched by a magnet turns toward the poles of the world; the eighth, how a magnet attracts iron; the ninth, how the northern part attracts the southern and vice versa; the tenth, on the inquiry into where the magnet receives the natural power that it possesses. Of the second part, the chapters are: the first is on the construction of an instrument by which the position of the sun, moon, and other stars is found; the second is on the construction of another, better instrument for the same purpose; the third is on the entire artifice of the construction of perpetual motion <note>The author, Petrus Peregrinus, is describing one of the earliest recorded attempts to create a "perpetual motion" machine using magnetic force.</note>.

## Chapter One

Dearest of friends, having been requested by you, I am writing to you in a simple narrative concerning a certain hidden nature of the magnetic stone <term>magnetic stone: the lodestone, a naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite</term>. For since nothing is aptly demonstrated by philosophers in the middle of a subject without knowledge of the first principle <unclear>is shown</unclear>...

deprived, and the nature of good things is darkened, until it is raised up by the rays of the heart's teachings. However, to treat of the hidden <note>original: "occultis"; the secret or esoteric properties</note> aspects of this stone belongs to the art of stone-carving; and although these works will be manifest to anyone accustomed to them, they will nonetheless seem to the common people like illusions and fantasies. Therefore, as far as the public is concerned, they are "sciences," but to astrologers and natural philosophers they will be sufficiently manifest. For this reason, that which is shown through his work—a manual effect—he achieves through his own industry, where even a small error poses a risk. Add to this that he could not achieve these things through natural science and mathematics alone if the industry of the hands were lacking. For in optical works <note>original: "ocularibus opibus"; likely referring to the creation of lenses or mirrors</note> we have great need of manual industry, and for the most part, the work would be better completed without it, for many things would be subject to wondrous sights which we cannot complete by hand alone. From these things, it is clear what sort of person the practitioner of this work ought to be.

# On the Recognition of the Stone

This stone is recognized in four ways: <term>namely</term> <note>Latin: scilicet</note> by its color, its homogeneity, its weight, and its power. Its color ought to be a leaden iron-gray, mixed with indigo or a sky-blue hue, so that it appears like polished iron tarnished by corrupted air. Indeed, I have never seen such a stone without great efficacy. Such a stone is most often found in northern regions, such as Normandy and Flanders. 

Furthermore, this stone ought to be homogeneous in its substance. One that has rusty spots and <unclear>pitted</unclear> holes is not of the highest quality, though a magnet is rarely found without some roughness. Such a stone—which, due to its homogeneity and the fine arrangement of its subtle parts, has become heavy—should be found to be of greater weight relative to its size. Its power, moreover, is known through its strong attraction of iron of great weight, the method of which will be described further below. If, therefore, you find a stone with these characteristics, obtain it if you can. These, then, are the ways by which the knowledge of this stone is gathered.

## Chapter Four

### Chapter Five

Regarding the way of knowing the poles of the stone <term>Tyrie</term> <note>likely a reference to the magnet or "Therian" stone</note>: which of them is the northern and which is the southern, you shall know by this method. Take a wooden vessel made in the manner of a cup or a deep dish, and place the stone in it so that the two points of the stone are equidistant from the edge of the vessel. Then place that vessel, with the stone set inside, into another large vessel full of water, so that the stone in the first vessel is like a sailor in a ship. Let the first vessel be in the second with ample space, like a ship floating in a river; and let there be plenty of space so that the natural motion of the stone is not hindered by contact with the edge of the large vessel. For the stone, placed in this way, will turn its first vessel until the northern pole of the stone stands directly facing the northern pole of the heavens, and the southern pole stands directly facing the southern pole. If it were moved away a thousand times, a thousand times it would return to its place by the will of God. And since the northern and southern parts are known in the heavens, the points in the stone will be known, because any part of the stone will be directly aligned with its corresponding part of the heavens.

### Chapter Six

Once you have gained knowledge of which pole in the stone is the north <note>original: "septentrionalis"</note> and which is the south <note>original: "meridionalis"</note>, mark the poles with engravings so that you may recognize them whenever necessary. And if you wish, afterwards observe how stone attracts stone. You shall arrange two stones prepared as has been described in this manner: place one in its vessel so that it floats like a sailor in a ship <note>The author uses the "floating magnet" method, where a lodestone is placed in a wooden bowl in water to allow it to rotate freely.</note>, and let the points already found be equidistant from the horizon or the rim of the vessel. 

Hold the other stone in your hand and bring the north part of the stone you are holding near to the south part of the stone floating in the vessel. The floating stone will indeed follow the stone you hold, as if wishing to cling to it. And if you present the south part of the stone you are carrying <insert>in your hand</insert> toward the north part of the floating stone, the same thing will happen, namely that the floating stone follows the stone you hold. 

Know therefore as a rule that the north part in a stone seeks the south in another stone, and the south seeks the north. And if you do the opposite—namely, if you bring north near to north—the stone you carry in your hand will seem to put the floating stone to flight. And if you join south to south, the same will happen. This is because the north part desires the south, and therefore it is seen to flee the north. The proof of this is that it will finally join with the south. The opposite happens regarding the remaining part, namely the south, which if <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the logic of magnetic repulsion on the next page.</note>

## Chapter Seven

It is known to all experienced men that when an oblong piece of iron <term>ferrum: iron, specifically a needle or rod in this context</term> has touched a magnet and has been fastened to a light piece of wood or a stick and placed in water, one part will move toward the star which they call the "nautical star" <note>The North Star, Polaris</note> because it is near the pole. For the truth is that it does not move toward the said star, but toward the pole (the proof of which we have asserted in its own chapter previously); the remaining part moves toward the opposite part of the heavens. But as for which part of the iron moves toward which part of the heavens, you should know that the part of the iron which the southern part of the stone touches will turn toward the north of the heavens. Conversely, it will be the case for the part of the iron which the northern part of the stone has touched; it will turn toward the south. This is a thing to be demonstrated to one who does not understand the cause of this motion, an experiment which we have set down truly and at length. Now at last, having set aside points *a* and *b*, we consider what remains. For that which holds point *d* is left behind. If it is exposed to water <note>The author refers to the common medieval practice of floating a magnet on a piece of wood in water to allow it to rotate freely toward the poles.</note>, it will be seen that *d* is the southern part, just as it was at first, because it will turn toward the south. The remaining part, however, from the side of the fracture, will be the northern part, which is *c*. Therefore, this stone will be *c-d*, whereas previously it was *a-d*.

And so, this first stone *a-b* acts as the <term>agent</term><note>The active force or "mover" in a physical interaction.</note>, and *c-d* as the <term>patient</term><note>The object being acted upon or receiving the influence.</note>. Thus it will be seen that two parts of two stones, which before their separation were continuous as one stone, are called one northern and the other southern after separation. 

And if these parts are again brought near to one another, one attracts the other, and they are joined together at points *b* and *c* where the fracture occurred. From this—as much as is possible by natural appetite <note>The "natural appetite" refers to the inherent tendency of objects to return to their natural state or place.</note>—they become one body as they were at first. The proof of this is that if they are worked there, they exhibit the same opposition as before. The agent, therefore, as I see by experiment, drives its patient to be united with itself. Similarly, this happens by reason of the likeness between them.

It is necessary, therefore, when *b* is joined with *c* by the northern virtue, that one line be made from the agent and the patient; otherwise, following this order, let it be *a-b-c-d* so that *b* and *c* are a single point. In this union, the <term>identity</term><note>original: "ydemptitas." The state of remaining the same or maintaining the same properties.</note> of the extreme parts is retained or preserved in the likeness in which they were before. For *a* is northern in the whole line just as it was when undivided; in the same way, the southern part remains in the divided patient just as it was when united with the other. Indeed, *b* and *c* are made into the same thing. And in the same way...

It happens that if *a* is joined with *d*, two lines become one through the power of a single spirit of action <note>The "spirit of action" refers to the unified magnetic force that governs the newly joined stone</note> according to this order: *c, r, d, a, r, b*. Since *d* and *a* are a single point, the integrity of the outer parts will remain just as they were before they were united. For *a* was the northern point and *b* was the southern, just as *b* and *c* were when separate. 

If, however, it were done otherwise, the identity or similarity of the parts would not be preserved. You see, for instance, that if *c* were joined with *a*—which follows from the union—one line would be formed from those two lines according to this order: *b, a, c, d*. If they are joined at one point *a*, which was southern before it was moved, it is found in this total line that *b*, the remaining extremity, becomes northern, though it was previously southern. 

Behold, the identity or similarity of the parts is destroyed! Or, if *b* were placed as southern just as it was before they were united, it would require that *d*, the other part, exist as northern, even though it had been southern. And thus, the identity and similarity shown through that divided piece is not preserved, even though the whole should gradually be of the same acting species <note>original: "specie agente"; referring to the specific nature or essence of the magnetic force</note>. This would not be the case if nature chose that impossible path. 

The same inconvenience would happen if one joined *b* with *d* so that one line was made according to this order: *a, b, d, c*. And because for the sender <note>The "sender" or "prime mover" in medieval physics refers to the natural law or Creator</note>—for everything that tends toward being acts in the best way that it can—it chooses the first order of action in which identity is better preserved than in the second. 

It is clear, therefore, from these things why the southern attracts the northern, and likewise why the southern never attracts the southern, nor the northern the northern, by nature.

# In the name of the Lord, amen. Here begins the book of Philo on
# the ingenuity of waters.

In the name of God, the pious and merciful, begins the book of Philo on spiritual <note>original: "spiritualibus," here referring to pneumatics or the science of air and spirits</note> devices. Because you said, my friend Ariston <note>original: "arguthoni," likely a corruption of Ariston, the traditional addressee of Philo's work</note>, that you now have a desire to understand subtle engineering, I, being subject to your will, respond to your questioning and willingly acquiesce to your request for the composition of this book. I establish this entire treatise for your diligent study so that in all matters regarding these types of inventions, you may have a useful guide. Desiring to treat these matters, I assert first of all that the knowledge of these things was known to many of the wise. Wherefore the philosophers who have considered natural matters, not consenting to the erroneous opinion of the many, have said that no vessel is empty in the way that people think, but is full of either air or some other body. I, however, desiring to enjoy brevity <gloss>with</gloss> in the present business, wish to treat this without introducing their words or their dissonant objections at present, lest my discourse fall into a tedious plurality. It is indeed clearly demonstrated and apparent to the sense of sight that air is one of the primary elements. This is first manifest to us and falls under our senses, not merely in name. Regarding these things, it shall suffice to speak to manifest what I intend, and I shall confirm that air is a body. For if you take a vessel which you think to be empty, shaped so that it is wide in the middle and narrow at the top, specifically in the manner of an amphora <note>A tall ancient Greek or Roman jar with two handles and a narrow neck</note>.

Concerning the vessel from which wine is tasted: when someone holds the opening of this vessel in their mouth, by sucking they draw in the air that is present; and along with the air, the soft and very liquid substance <note>The wine</note> that lies beneath is drawn up, because it is joined to the air as if it were attached by glue or some other binding. # On the Expansion of Air by Heat

The vessel should not be too thin, lest it break easily, nor should it be too heavy, provided it is well-dried so that our desired result is better achieved. Then, let it be perforated at the top and a pipe <term>canalis; a tube or siphon</term> be inserted into it. Let the end of this pipe descend all the way to the bottom. Let the other end of the same pipe be placed into another vessel full of water, almost to the bottom as in the first, so that the flow is improved. Let the ball be marked **a**, the pipe **b**, and the full vessel **c**.

I say, therefore, that if you place the ball in the sun, when it has become heated, a portion of the air enclosed within will exit through the pipe. This will be evident in practice because the air will fall from the pipe into the water, mixing with it and creating many bubbles <note>original: "ampullas"; literally flasks or bubbles</note> one after another. 

If, however, the ball is placed back in the shade, or anywhere where the sun's ray <note>original: "radius solis"</note> does not reach, the water will ascend through the pipe until it descends into the ball. Afterward, if you place it back in the sun, the water will return into the other vessel; and if you do the opposite, it will always happen in this manner as often as you repeat it. Furthermore, if you heat the ball with fire, the same result will occur; or even if you pour hot water over the ball, provided it has not yet cooled, the air will exit.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of pneumatic principles, specifically addressing the impossibility of a vacuum in nature.</meta>

What I am about to say is similar to the previous mechanical principle, and this occurs only because a vacuum <note>Latin: "locus vacuus," a space containing nothing</note> cannot exist. For if it were emptied of air, another body joined to that air would immediately follow and take its place, because they are driven by a prevailing nature. The learned professors of sacred matters <note>Likely a reference to Scholastic theologians who argued "Nature abhors a vacuum"</note> assert this, and we hold a similar opinion. Therefore, we shall demonstrate that a space cannot be empty of air or any other body.

An example of this is as follows: if we take water in a vessel labeled **a**, and in its center stands an object labeled **b** in the manner of a lampstand, upon which we place a candle—let it be labeled **c**—and light it. Over this, we <unclear>place</unclear> a vessel labeled **d**, so that its mouth is near the water and the candle is positioned in its center. You will see shortly thereafter that the water which was in the lower vessel rises up into the upper vessel. This would not happen except for the reason we mentioned: because the air contained in that vessel, through the fire of the ascent, cannot endure with the fire. After that air has perished through the motion of the fire, it happens that the water is raised according to the quantity of what perished.

And this phenomenon is similar to what happens to a drinking animal <note>A reference to the mechanics of suction in biology</note> if the air above the drink in this candle-vessel is consumed; because it becomes "aged," so to speak, being thinned out by the fire. Therefore, the succeeding water is raised and its place, which was becoming empty, is suddenly filled. This is the established science of this matter, and it is evident to the senses.

It is certainly established that if one part of a tube is placed in a vessel full of water and the other part is raised <note>The text describes the action of a siphon where the external arm must be lower than the internal water level to function.</note>, all the water will be emptied until the vessel is drained by that pipe. Note that <term>burning water</term><note>original: "aqua ardens"; an early term for distilled alcohol or brandy</note> is of two kinds: simple and composite.

# On the Water of Life

...naval pitch, turpentine, common oil,
<term>sal ammoniac</term><note>original: "sal mnr" (sal ammoniacum); a salt used in alchemy and medicine</note>, common salt, mastic, honey, <term>euphorbium</term><note>a medicinal resin derived from spurge plants</note>,
soap, <term>opopanax</term><note>a gum resin used in perfumes and medicine</note>, <term>pyrite</term><note>original: "pirit' capari'"; likely copper or iron pyrites</note>, <term>squama aeris</term><note>original: "squā ti"; copper scales or flakes</note>,
<term>spodium</term><note>ash or residue from burnt minerals or ivory</note>, white pepper, black pepper, and long pepper,
<term>castoreum</term><note>a secretion from beavers used in medicine</note>, <term>zedoary</term><note>an aromatic root similar to ginger</note>; of each of these, mix well with good musk and ambergris, with the bone of a stag's heart <note>a common medieval remedy for heart ailments</note> of each a similar amount, as it shall be seen.

Many philosophers and masters of medicine have discovered and handed down how much this "water of life" <note>original: "aqua vite"; distilled spirits or brandy used as a solvent for medicines</note> is to be used, for it is a chosen and healthy medicine among all others. Its use preserves one from every infirmity that is not fatal, and consequently, it preserves one from every fatal death—especially those that are sudden and unnatural. For it gives nourishment to the body, restores health, guards the digestion, and strengthens the virtue <note>the "vital power" or "faculty"</note> against harmful influences.

For the philosophers say that no medicine has been found that is so supportive and augmentative of the natural heat as is this water of life, because of the familiarity and fellowship it has with human nature, and because it is suitable for human bodies. Its heat is similar to natural heat, and it transforms the blood into a pure and clean state. And it not only strengthens the natural heat, but also clarifies turbid blood, and leads the matter of the veins to all the members of the body with sufficient appetite. It cleanses obstructions of the liver, removes the cloudiness of the eyes, expels sadness from the body, and corroborates all the members of the body.

And its virtue works not only in the body, but also in the soul; it alleviates distress and forgetfulness, and confers memory, sharpness of mind, and boldness.
